subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while it takes some time to get organized on Monday morning, we are here to discuss Bill C-143, which is a Bill to give the Government more borrowing authority. It is not a pleasure to speak to this Bill. We are reminded once again that our national financial affairs are in a sorry state. Those who are supposedly in charge of the country and fiddling while Canada groans.
When I spoke on this Bill during another stage of its debate, I dealt with many of the problems that are becoming even more persistent and critical than they were at that time. Many of my colleagues have discussed other aspects of the Bill from their own perspective. We are now faced with another stage of debate on this Bill to grant additional borrowing powers to the Government for an exceptionally large amount of money which, I understand, is the largest amount to be asked for in our history.
I would like to bring to the attention of the House a statement made by the present President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) back on October 23, 1979. At that time he stated that the Government-speaking of the Progressive Conservative Government at the time-should move quickly to present its budget. He said that it should be a budget which contained measures of a focused and specific nature designed to help our economy become more productive and efficient and deal with our deficit in current accounts.
I suggest that that is a very significant statement. The Government at that time seemed to be very concerned about some of these problems, whereas the present Government seems to have allowed those issues and concerns to fade into the background rather than dealing with them specifically at a time when it has the opportunity to do so.
There are two specific areas of concern to which reference has been made. The first concern is that of productivity. When I spoke to this Bill on Tuesday, March 1, I made reference to this particular aspect of the problem. 1 believe it is absolutely essential that an emphasis on increased productivity be made a priority. If productivity cannot be increased in Canada, we will not be able to deal with other problems effectively and efficiently.
While there has been a great deal of discussion about Government policies and the allocation of funds to various programs, we must remember that the Government will only be able to do this through the redistribution of funds from the resources that are already available unless productivity is increased. Instead of raising the standard of living and increasing the viability of our economy, the funds will just be spread around a little more and will therefore reduce the average standard of living of the people of Canada. Therefore, I am afraid that the Government has done little, if anything, to achieve an improvement in the productivity of the country.
[DOT] (mo)
The second phase as set out by the Minister at that time addressed deficits. He said that the budget should contain measures to help our economy become "more efficient and to deal with our deficit in current account". The only way the Government is dealing with it is by increasing it. This is certainly not acceptable to the Canadian people at the present time. If the Government continues with its deficits, as it is doing, and if it increases taxation and all the ill-effects of such a program, then it will not improve the economy, as it must do.

One of the costs is the ever-increasing interest burden. Then there is the loss of flexibility because in many respects, the Government is pretty well boxed in and unable to respond to the various situations which arise.
The third cost arising from such a program involves private sector borrowings which are crowded out. Then, of course, there is the loss of confidence on the part of the Canadian people. This is another serious ill effect as far as continuing deficit financing is concerned. An article in the Ottawa Citizen of February 21, 1983 states:
The more the federal Government is forced to spend in bad times, the longer better times will be delayed: the money needed to finance Government deficits will be found at the expense of the private sector, and the resulting competition for funds will drive up interest rates.
I should like to point out that some time ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made a statement that a new morality must be established in dealing with international affairs. I suggest that there ought to be on the national level, as well. 1 would ask: Because a particular Party in the House has a majority, is it moral for it continually to overspend and then force Canadians to bear an ever-increasing burden of taxation to support unconscionable borrowings to finance the Government's profligate spending? I would answer no.
Secondly, is it moral to build up a staggering burden of debt for our children, our grandchildren and generations beyond that, which they will be called upon to bear, as well as financing the affairs of Government in the particular period in which they live? Again, I say no.
Therefore, as we consider this particular Bill today, I would take the same stand I took before, and that is that I believe that the Government has not established any credibility and does not deserve our authorizing borrowing authority for this amount.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no way, without inviting criticism, that any Member of this House of Commons could with clear conscience vote for this Bill at this moment in time.
Let me cite some of the reasons it is impossible for me to support this Bill. In view of the imbalanced expenditure which is, first, exercised in respect to the fisheries in the Province of New Brunswick, my criticism is not of the extent of the expenditure in other constituencies than my own. My criticism
is that my own constituency has been neglected in this expenditure, particularly in the small craft harbours structure. When we look at the Estimates that are presently before the Committees of this House and see that $5 million and $6 million projects have been undertaken on the northeast coast of New Brunswick, while there is not an expenditure of consequence, which will even be listed, on the Bay of Fundy shore of New Brunswick, I submit to you that the inferences are obvious and do not have to be specified in my remarks.
This is causing fishermen in my constituency to fish from moorings which are just not up to standard, which are damaging their boats and which are detrimental to the development or even the conduct of the existing business which takes place on a very significant scale among thousands of my constituents.
Secondly, in respect to the fishery, let me point out that regulations are changed without notice to the fishermen. The latest example is that lobster fishermen in my constituency had been authorized to set their traps and to fish between the traffic lanes of the deep sea traffic which goes in and out of the port of Saint John. The stipulations, when they were first given permission to fish there, were as follows: "Yes, you may fish there and, secondly, you are strictly at your own risk. The Department or the Government at large will take no responsibility for the safety of the people, the safety of the boat or the gear itself. But under those conditions you may fish between the shipping lanes in the Bay of Fundy as they lead to Saint John."
About ten days ago the Department of Fisheries, without any notice, after lobster gear had already been set, notified the fishermen that they must get out of that space between the traffic lanes in the Bay of Fundy. This brings on new and unnecessary hardships to the fishing industry of my area. And I am supposed to vote for that?
Let me also point out that surveillance by the Department of Fisheries is lax and incompetent. Last week, on one day, two large scallop draggers from the United States were fishing five miles within the recognized fishing line between Canada and the United States. If our surveillance is so bad that we cannot in fact apprehend boats which are five miles within Canadian waters, well outside the legal limits for any American ship, then there is something seriously wrong.
Let me indicate the consequence of such an infringment upon our rights. There is no fishery which is as profitable at this moment as the scallop fishery, and there is no area where better scallops exist than in these beds. We are allowing these scallops to be taken illegally, without any apprehension or any charges laid, day after day in the area of fishing as it relates to my constituency.
Not only are the regulations coming without notice and infringing upon the rights of our fishermen, but the regulations are not consistent, nor are they consistently applied.
Another item with respect to the fishery is that the Department of Transport has without notice chosen to widen one of the traffic lanes by one and one half miles. When you are
March 28, 1983

working from an island, with very little sea space in which to fish, and you lose a mile and a half of it without notice, you have certainly lost a lot of fishing opportunity. Those on the other side of this House want me to vote for a Bill to borrow more money to govern in that fashion? No way, Mr. Speaker.
I want to mention the potato industry. There is in process under the leadership of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) an effort to organize an eastern Canadian potato marketing agency. There are questions unanswered which must be answered. They are drawn from the examples which have been set by the Canadian Dairy Commission and by CEMA, the protector of the egg industry in Canada. What are those words that I have?
Under the Canadian Dairy Commission, there have been several instances of processors of cheese saying they could not get enough milk under this structure to produce their historic quantity of cheese, nor could they get enough milk to make cheese to supply the demand which they presently have. If that is the way quotas are to be allocated under a marketing system, it just will not work for the potato industry.
When we come to the egg industry, we find that there are those who have made an effort to export eggs from Canada. They have not even had consideration by the various provincial boards, nor by the national board, whether there is an opportunity for egg exports. There are on occasion surpluses of eggs in Canada. We should be ready to explore the export market. These surpluses of eggs are burdensome and costly to the producer and consumer alike. I do not want to see the same situation develop in the potato industry.
In the egg industry, there is a regulation whereby you can raise X number of hens which you may market outside the agency. If such a regulation is to be introduced into any eastern Canadian potato marketing board, there are questions we have to ask. What is the minimum number of acres of potatoes which can be produced without coming under the regulation of the quota? If there is such a regulation, how many members of how many families will be able to plant up to that amount of potatoes? I would assume for the moment that it might be five acres of potatoes that could be produced without regulation under such a marketing principle as CEMA or the way the dairy board presently functions. If that be the case, how many members of a large family will be able to produce potatoes on five acres and what impact will this have on the market?
The next question is, how can you regulate the production and marketing of any agricultural product when only God, who controls the weather, can tell you what your yield will be? You do not know that until you harvest because He does not tell you in advance. How are you going to handle the situation in which you have unusually good crops of any fruit or vegetable across Canada, particularly potatoes? How are you going to supply Canada in the years when you have an unusually poor crop across Canada? Production has been known to fluctuate by as much as 25 per cent in two years in Canada. That is the exception. It may be 25 per cent up or 25 per cent

down from the historic rate of production, not necessarily because of more or less acres but because of weather conditions as they exist in the areas in which the product is produced.
We are now having meetings in Atlantic Canada trying to establish an eastern Canadian potato agency. I want the Minister of Agriculture to answer these questions. What is he putting forward besides propaganda for these people to work with in reality? What is he doing to them except constraining the payments which historically have been made to underpaid farmers for their production? All the Minister is doing is constraining those payments in order to compel hard-up farmers to join the eastern potato agency. How on the basis of the cheese factories and egg marketing can a processor of potatoes be assured of a given supply of potatoes for his business? How is he going to be able to support an export market which he may have developed and which may be, and probably is, a fluctuating market requiring different sizes of demand? He cannot know in April of any given year what he is going to require from the potato crop in his area 12, 13, 15 months down the road, which is the supply he must accommodate during his producing years.
How are we going to know if we have to abandon the seed export markets, which are also variable? How are we going to achieve a balance which will supply our table requirements? Are we going to ban imports into Canada entirely for the table market? If so, of course, we ban the opportunity to export from Canada. Without proper storage capabilities, how are we going to supply Canada 12 months a year?
I would like to ask something else, which I have repeatedly asked in the House because of my deep concern. What voice is Atlantic Canada going to have? Will it be a five-Province organization with a vote each, or will it be an organization which, in any other structure outside of Government, would grant to any area the number of votes which relates to their productivity? With respect to the stock they hold in the business, roughly 50 per cent of the area is supplied by New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. Are they then to have roughly 50 per cent of the voting control? If they do not, New Brunswick and P.E.I. will be in serious shape.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have reached a deficit and borrowing crisis because this Government is labouring under the illusion which has pervaded western economic thought for the past 40 years; that is, that the demand for goods creates its own supply, that the demand for goods can be increased by increasing the purchasing power of individuals by deficit financing or money creation. As a result, the deficit today is equal to 28 per cent of all Government expenditure. For every four dollars which the Government spends, it must borrow one more dollar to finance that spending.
There are only two ways to finance this deficit, either by printing money and debasing the currency, which has currently

March 28, 1983
Borrowing Authority
fallen to a base of 80 cents U.S., or by borrowing more money and thus ever increasing the deficit. This is a pattern which has been followed year after year, in good years and in bad years, this constant borrowing and escalation of the deficit. The interest burden on financing the deficit costs each individual- and that is just interest alone-$700 per year, or $16.7 billion. This constitutes in itself 4.8 per cent of Canada's Gross National Product.
It is interesting that in fact this interest burden is equal to the loss in GNP which we experienced during the last year. This effectively reduces private sector stimulation of the economy which is, of course, the engine of economic growth. It does this in three ways: first, it increases the tax burden for Canadians; second, it crowds out the private sector borrowing which is a proven job creater; and, third, productivity and growth are hampered by a crisis in confidence in the investment community instilled by the actions of a fiscally confused and irresponsible Government which continues to debase the Canadian currency through excessive Government borrowing.
Government borrowing for job creation is working effectively to ensure that real jobs, based on economic growth and increased productivity, are in fact being squeezed out, and will continue to be squeezed out as long as we keep this deficit process building, growing and increasing at such a ridiculous rate. As a result of this, the dollar falls, the cost of living goes up, interest rates continue to be high and job-creating capital investment seeks more friendly and lucrative atmospheres.
What is the way that Canada can redress this fiscally irresponsible philosophy? How can we bring economic prosperity and growth and, therefore, social justice to this land? Is the answer to be found in a Government which believes in a program of taxing and spending the country to the brink of bankruptcy? Is that the policy? I do not think so. Is the answer to borrow more and more to pay ever-increasing deficit payments on which you must keep borrowing again and again to pay in ever-increasing spirals? No, Mr. Speaker, these are not the answers. These are the policies of the Government, but they are not the answers to the economic crisis which is facing us today.
Creating jobs and ensuring humanitarian social assistance to those in need in these difficult recessionary economic times will occur if the Government concentrates on ensuring that real revenues rise. That is the only way it can happen. You cannot just keep borrowing; you have to create a climate of productivity, and from that tax revenues will flow to the Government. That is the way the problem has to be cured, rather than by borrowing and borrowing. The answer does lie in productivity and growth.
This country is a land of great human and natural resource potential. It can recover, but only if we reverse current Government economic trends. The way to do that is by changing the entire thought process, the mindset. What is important is not the creation of more money, but rather the creation of more real wealth. The essence of a sound, prosperous economy
is not the quantity of money but, rather, the quality of money; the purchasing power of the dollar is more important than the number of dollars you in fact have. So many of us have experienced that personally or through our constituents. They perhaps have or make a lot of money, but what does it buy for them? Virtually less and less each year.
The key to economic recovery and prosperity for Canadians is, therefore, not for this Government to borrow more and spend more, because the mindset of this Government is impoverished by the lethargic, self-serving, bureaucratic and unproductive growth that hampers the true growth of the Canadian individual. Instead of taxing and spending, we have to put more money into people's hands which they can spend on consumer products and create jobs to get the economy and the Canadian people working again. The wrong people are borrowing and spending; the wrong people are, directly and indirectly, saving and investing, and lending to, the wrong people in the wrong institutions. People are lending their money to financial institutions; the institutions then tend to lend it back to Government, and then Government tries to redistribute it to the people of Canada. That process has to be reversed. What has to be done is for the Government to create a climate of confidence so that the people who are putting their money into savings right now will have enough confidence in the private sector, the individual small-businessman, to put that money into his hands to create more real jobs, more growth and more productivity.
We hear a lot about the plight of farmers, Mr. Speaker. Well, that is a very real plight. We have had a special emergency debate on this subject. I think that was important and 1 support it. But what about the small-businessman who is in exactly the same position? Our institutions and Government in turn are taking the small business generators of real jobs, growth and productivity, and just pulling them under faster and faster through bankruptcy and receivership.
It is time to give small business a chance. They have been creating jobs for 20 years and it is time for the Government of Canada to encourage borrowing by those small businesses to help them survive the economic crunch. Just get them over the next six months and then we can tag on to the American recovery, which is where part of the answer to our own growth problems lies. But the Government will not create that needed climate of confidence by taking more and more out of the economy through increased borrowing. That is not going to work. It is not the right measure at this time.
The key to economic recovery and prosperity for Canadians is to increase productivity itself. I think if I just stood here and said that the key is to increase productivity itself, and repeated it 5,000 times, that might be the way to create the kind of mindset we have to create in the Government. Productivity will occur once we cut the Gordian knot of Government growth and private sector stagnation. Canada's Gross National Product has the potential to be the most impressive of the OECD nations, but we are outstripping them all only in our own dismal performance of being twenty-fourth out of 24
March 28, 1983

nations. The growth in our GNP is a grotesquely negative 5 per cent, a full 1.5 per cent less than the next worse nation.
I want to know how this additional borrowing of another $19 billion is going to improve our performance. 1 do not understand how it will and I have not been told by anyone on the Government side. These GNP figures mean jobs have been lost for Canadians as the unemployment lines swell to 1.6 million, or 12.4 per cent of the work force. In British Columbia the figure is even higher at 14.2 per cent, and that is the very lowest estimate rather than the reality. The number of people looking for work is much, much higher.
These people, Mr. Speaker, must be given work so that they can fulfil themselves as individuals and help this nation prosper and grow. The American economy is starting to recover; 1983 will be a year of economic success due to lower tax rates, interest rates and energy prices. Canada has the opportunity to ride this wave of prosperity but instead the Government is borrowing its way into penury and poverty. The Government is flirting with the danger of structural deficits which will be endemic to our economic system and mortgage the future of our children and grandchildren. We can prevent this. We can bring prosperity and growth, jobs and economic renewal to this land by going back to the basics. This Bill is a further step away from sound economic policy and a better way of life for all Canadians, and on that basis I am unable to support it or the philosophy which has placed this unfortunate tragedy on Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I have always listened intently to the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman). Sometimes I hear things I like to hear, sometimes things I disagree with, but one way or another I always react. I must say to him as one who has spoken very loudly and clearly in support of Reaganomics that the world recession we are in-and it is a world recession, not a Canadian recession-can be blamed in large part on the policies of the U.S. Government, particularly those of the Reagan Government and its failure to get interest rates down at the rate I think they should come down.
I must say that the tax cuts the U.S. Government brought in have a very large bearing on the U.S. deficit. Studies that I have seen, particularly one done by a group at the University of Toronto Institute for Policy Analysis, indicate that our deficit is a recession deficit and that if the recession had not happened-in other words, if we could go back to 1979 when we had a reasonable growth picture-we would actually have a small surplus this year. The U.S. Government figures are quite different. The tax cuts and very large defence expenditures increase have created a situation where they would have a deficit in the order of $90 billion to $100 billion in any given year.

Borrowing Authority

Member and I hope we are approaching it in a genuine manner. I would advocate an increase in surplus over a short period of time in order to create employment and to stimulate the economy which, in the long run, should reduce the deficit. Some economists-and Informetrica is one-have conducted studies which indicate that the deficit will be reduced this year by about $5 billion because the economy is beginning to show some degree of improvement. I do not think stimulation will hurt the economy but, rather, will do some good.
I am also concerned about the fact that we have a long-term unemployment problem which must be faced. Even if the deficit were brought back to zero this year by a large growth factor, most economists tell us that 11 or 12 per cent of the population would still be unemployed, more or less on a permanent basis. The real problem is how to change that to not more than perhaps 6 or 7 per cent unemployment, taking into account those people who move between one job and another. With the present unemployment rate of 12 or 13 per cent, which we are told could continue for an indefinite period, we know that a large percentage of the population is not plugged in to the labour market. That means that basically they are not part of our society. The real problem is not the case of someone who is laid off for a few months, collects Unemployment Insurance benefits, then finds a job and is back in the labour force but, rather, those people who are not able to plug in to the labour market and who may be deprived of being part of the mainstream of Canadian life for most of their lives.
When we talk of unemployment we must take into account the young people in the 17 to 25 age bracket where the unemployment rate is about 30 or 35 per cent. We are talking about the young people coming on the labour market who do not find jobs and thus do not become part of the mainstream of society.
This is the real damage that is being done by the monetarists who claim that the economy must be slowed down to prevent inflation and all this unemployment. I have no problem with their concern about inflation. It is the cause of high interest rates and it creates all kinds of serious problems. However, there are other ways to eliminate inflation. One method is through the control mechanism. Another is to let the dollar float downward if necessary in order to keep interest rates down.
The problem that must be faced right away in this country is the large number of people who cannot find jobs. In my community of Thunder Bay the unemployment rate has been between 15 and 18 per cent for the last four or five months. It is rather difficult to interpret the figures because samples are very small, but a large number of people in the community just cannot find work at all. There is some hope that the housing

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thanks to the amendment put forward by the Conservative Party, this is the second time I have had the opportunity to make an intervention on Bill C-143. When I first addressed the Bill I spoke about the unemployment problem and the transition the country is going through, from the traditional industrial base that we have known for the last hundred years to the informational or high-tech aspect of our society.
Today I want to refer to one particular industry in order to give some idea of how short-sighted and wrong the present fiscal and monetary policies of the Government are with respect to borrowing. I refer to the farm implement industry which affects my riding, among others. Agricultural machinery used to be built not only in Brantford but in Chatham, Hamilton, Winnipeg and other centres in the country, so this is not a problem of central Canada but a nation-wide problem. Of course, the parts industry is also affected.
In 1982, the last year for which we have figures, we had a net deficit in agricultural implements of $985.4 million, just short of $1 billion. This is an absolute disgrace, Mr. Speaker. In 1981 the deficit was almost $2 billion, but the reduction is due to the fact that farmers do not have enough money to buy farm machinery. The roughly $1 billion which is represented here represents about 10,000 jobs in the agri-industry that should have been created in Canada but were not, even in a severe depression year, such as in 1982.
We often talk about the auto pact and its deficiencies. Generally speaking, over the years Canada has been a net loser in the auto pact as you can see if you go back to the mid-1960s, Mr. Speaker. We are also net losers year over year in farm implement manufacturing. I do not know why. We have a long record of making farm implements in this country. We
can go back to the early days of the Masseys, the Fergusons, the Harrises and the famous Cockshutt family from Brantford. We have made very fine implements and yet we have a net deficit in this industry. Last year we lost 10,000 jobs. When we talk about unemployment and the loss of 10,000 jobs or 20,000 jobs, it really does not mean an awful lot unless you relate those numbers to a certain community. Let me take Brantford as an example. We have had on balance for the past two years, at any given time, except perhaps the spring of 1982 and the spring of 1981, some 5,000 agricultural implement employees out of work. That situation affects approximately 15,000 to
20.000	people in a community whose total population is 75,000 and is an absolute economic disaster. It is also a social disaster in many respects as well. The Government's policies allowed
10.000	jobs in that farm implement industry to be exported out of the country because of our net deficit of approximately $1 billion, but we could have handled easily half of the lost 10,000 jobs in Brantford with 5,000 on lay-off. That may be an oversimplification of the situation, but in terms of figures half of those 10,000 unemployed could have found work in the City of Brantford.
While we have 5,000 people on chronic, long-term unemployment, we have another very interesting situation developing. Again I am referring to my own constituency of Brantford which has two major industries, Massey-Ferguson and White Farm Implements. If those two industries were in financially better shape they would be using the time of the recession and their capital resources to tranfer into the high-tech field. Perhaps they could go into high-tech assembly, robotronics or micro-processing. There is no doubt in my mind that if either one or both of those industries survive, that is precisely what they will be doing in the next four or five years. It is estimated not only in farm machinery manufacturing but in all major manufacturing that at least 40 per cent of all assemblers now on lay-off will suffer permanent lay-off. In Brantford, 40 per cent represents about 2,000 workers.
Let us look at some other figures. For 1983-1984 the federal Government has budgeted $5.2 billion for research and development, most of which will be in high-tech. As I said when I spoke a couple of weeks ago on this same Bill, only $230 million has been budgeted for the skills programs, which in a sort of way addresses itself to the need for retraining in high-tech.
I will give you some specific examples, Mr. Speaker. If you are laid off at Massey-Ferguson today, whether you are an assembler, a mechanic or whatever, you may qualify first for a skills orientation program. If you are still on Unemployment Insurance, that Unemployment Insurance does not run out before the ILAP designation on July 27 and you find a seat at Mohawk College, you can remain on Unemployment Insurance at $200 a week. If you are married and have a couple of kids, you can probably just get by on that $200 a week. However, should you not be able to find a seat at Mohawk College at the Braneida campus or in Hamilton before July 27-and in all likelihood you will not because every seat is taken

for the next six months-and your Unemployment Insurance runs out, when you do get placed in a skills program for upgrading and high-tech training, your income while on that program drops to a maximum of $104 a week for a married man with two children. subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again we are under the guillotine as the debate on Bill C-143 draws to a close. I do not particularly like speaking with a guillotine over my head but I suppose we must do so when we are faced with a Government such as the one opposite, which is not particularly concerned about how matters are debated in the House. The Government makes no effort to listen to what the Opposition says and act upon that advice. Instead it comes forward with a Bill with the intention to bull it through, no matter what arguments are made by the other side.
The amendment which we are debating today would have the effect of allowing the Government, within what remains of this fiscal year, to borrow the $5 billion that it requests. We do not really quarrel with that since most of that money has already been spent. However, we would like to see the Government give more thought to its request for an additional $14 billion which it says it needs. In our opinion, the Government has not given enough consideration or thought to the effects of excessive borrowing.
In the few minutes that I have I would like to examine the effects of excessive borrowing. First, we must consider the cost of repayment, because I do not think the Government always takes this factor into account. It simply says that it needs the money and then asks to have authority to go to the capital markets of the country and borrow that money. But what about five or ten years down the road? The Government does not think about the consequences of its immediate action today.
The fact is that as one borrows and borrows and piles up more and more debt, the cost of servicing the debt goes up year by year. A couple of figures might be of interest. In the 196869 year, interest payments on the national debt amounted to 2 per cent of Gross National Product. I think that is a fairer way of putting it, rather than in dollar terms, because dollars have been affected by inflation. However, in the 1982-83 fiscal year, the interest on the debt will be 5 per cent of Gross National Product. We are pretty sure what it will be because we are nearly at the end of the fiscal year. The cost of repayment or the cost of interest on the public debt has increased by two and a half times since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office. The interest payments now amount to $1,700 per Canadian taxpayer.
Let us consider it from a slightly different perspective. Again, in 1968-69 one dollar in nine from federal revenues went toward debt servicing. In the period which is just ending, the 1982-83 fiscal year, it has been necessary to use one dollar in three from federal revenues solely for debt servicing. I wonder how much longer can we carry on along this road to ruin?
I was carefully listening to a speech given a few days ago on this very subject by the Hon. Member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain). He said that the Government is leaving a legacy of debt in Canada for generations and generations to come. It is doing this without proper thought or consideration.
It is funny that in Canada, a country which is so inherently wealthy, we are taxed to the hilt, yet we, speaking collectively, as Government, find ourselves with no money to spend. How can that be? There are billions of dollars generated from public revenues, but the Government never seems to have enough. That is obviously because it has not given proper consideration to the management of public affairs, and particularly to the management of public financial affairs in Canada. This is due to this borrowing which has taken place, greater and greater amounts each year, since 1968. Thirty per
March 28, 1983

cent or one-third of all the money which is now coming in is going toward servicing the debt which has piled up over the years since 1968.
This is why our social programs and services are going downhill and why we find ourselves without sufficient financial resources to maintain the health care standards to which we have been accustomed in this country. This is why useful public works are at a standstill.
1 was listening carefully to the Hon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) and he mentioned the fact that useful capital expenditures, which would pay dividends in the years to come, are not being made. They are not capable of being made because we have no money with which to make them. All that money, all that public revenue, has been used to service the debt. If we had looked after our affairs since 1968, public revenues would have been sufficient to make these necessary capital investments in roads, bridges, colleges and hospitals. In so doing, if that money had been invested for those purposes, it would have created the desperately needed employment in Canada.
Right now we are experiencing the worst of both worlds in this country because of past mismanagement. We are saddled with very high unemployment and we are unable to make those public investments which would have cut into that unemployment and created jobs for Canadians.
Another effect of the excessive borrowing of the present Liberal Government is that private borrowing is crowded out. In this country, there is at all times a bidding match going on within the capital markets for the available dollars, for the available savings. If Government comes into this market with such requirements as it has, $19 billion in this instance, and is prepared, because it must, to pay the high interest rates in order to attract that capital, then it is self-evident that there is no money left over for the private borrower, or he or she is forced to compete with these excessively high interest rates to get his or her share of the available savings. When the Government has a new bond issue, it must make the rate on that bond attractive; otherwise, people will not buy it. It must inch up the interest rate so as to attract people to lend money to the Government.
Most of the money the Government borrows, whether it is through Canada Savings Bonds or other obligations of the Government, is the accrued savings of Canadians. The Government is not using those savings for capital purposes; it is using them for current account purposes. What is actually happening in Canada is the destruction of capital. Canadians save and put by money, dollar by dollar perhaps $100 a month, and then the Government borrows that money. Instead of using it for capital purposes, it uses it for current account purposes, thereby destroying the accumulated capital. Private borrowers are priced out of the market.
Am I correct in assuming that my ten minutes has already expired? That being the case, I will give Your Honour the next thrilling instalment of this debate when my time comes up again tomorrow on third reading.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister, in his various remarks over the last week, has been

referring to consultation with regard to the budget and, shall we say, the whole of the Government's economic program. However, let us examine that in light of the requirements of this particular Bill. The Bill seeks borrowing authority of about $19 billion.

However, the Government has used the provisions of Section 39 of the Financial Administration Act. We have seen publicity in the newspapers to the effect that this is an obscure Section of the Financial Administration Act and that the process is perhaps somewhat strange or not often used. The Government, as the Minister said, has been going to the Treasury bill market every week. There is a reason why the Government has been going weekly to the Treasury bill market. These are short-term Treasury bills, usually a maximum of six months, but the Government is using this procedure, along with actions by the Bank of Canada, to control the movement of the interest rate. These are being used as a tool basically at the present time to keep the interest rate in Canada sufficiently higher than the interest rate in the United States so as to buttress the level of the Canadian dollar.
The Canadian dollar has been floating since 1971. Canada is not involved, as France was last week and indeed has been for many months prior to the events of last week, in trying to defend a certain level of the Canadian dollar against the fixed amount of the reserve U.S. dollar or against part of the monetary snake in Europe.
I say frankly that the Minister is conning the Canadian public by what he says about consultations in what was talked about by the former Minister of Finance in the budgetary statement of June 28. Consultation is consultation pure and simple. It is not talking things over after the event. Last summer's process of hearing public representations on the Ways and Means motion was not consultation. There were changes but that was not a result of consultation. Instead, it was hearing representations after proposals had been set down in quick-setting cement.
The Minister talks about consultations now in various areas with regard to the budget. How is that different from previous years? National associations, such as the Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and any number of other groups, have filed briefs with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) on the subject of budgetary provisions precisely as they are doing now. public more, but that is not the consultation that we would like to see.

He told us in October that he would present a budget some time during these weeks after which he would ask for borrowing authority, and that is a proper sequence. My colleague for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) had an amendment which would have eliminated Part II of the Bill, and that is precisely the position we are taking. He does not tell us when he is going to come forward with another borrowing Bill. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be speaking today to Bill C-143. The House is now considering an amendment proposed by the Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) which would in effect cut
the borrowing authority requested by the Government by about $14 billion. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) asked the House for a borrowing authority of $19 billion because the borrowing requirements for the financial year ending this week amounted to $5 billion, and because the projected deficit for 1982-83 was higher than expected. The Minister is asking for authority to borrow $14 billion more because he wants to ensure that the Government is able to carry out its debt program without disrupting financial markets. The Minister is requesting an additional authority of $14 billion for the first part of the 1983-84 financial year, not because he wants, as the previous Member told the House, a blank cheque, not because he wants Parliament to authorize him to borrow money he has no right to spend. Parliament must still authorize the Government's expenditures, and Parliament must determine how the Government is going to spend this money.
With its amendment, the Opposition is telling the Gover-ment that next week, when the next financial year begins, it will have to come back to Parliament to ask for another increase in order to be able to borrow $14 billion. Therefore, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) needs $19 billion and not just $5 billion. The Minister explained why in his speech to the House on February 17 of this year. He wants to ensure that when the Government starts borrowing on the money market, it can do so in an orderly manner without being obliged, as might happen, to borrow excessively large amounts during several weeks and thus put pressure on interest rates. Any Member of this House who is aware of the economic situation in this country at the present time will have to admit that between now and the months of June, July or August, 1983, it would be impossible to conduct Government operations otherwise than in a deficit situation. For instance, 72 per cent of the increase in the deficit since October last year was caused either by interest rates that were higher than expected when the loans were contracted or by a drop in Government revenue. In a recession, companies are making less money and as a result paying less in taxes. More workers are working shorter hours, and also paying less income tax. Many people are unemployed, so there are fewer people paying taxes, and as a result, Government revenue is not as high. It is the only way to change the situation by June, July or August, 1983. In fact, the Opposition wants to give the impression that the additional $14 billion requested by the Government for the next financial year is supposed to cover all the Government's borrowing requirements for 1983-84, which is not the case at all, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Finance made it clear in his speech on February 17 that it was only to cover requirements up to this summer, because whether we like it or not, the Government's deficit for 1983-84 may be as much as $24 or $25 billion. We hope that the recession has bottomed out and that we are now on our way to economic recovery. If that is the case, and if the encouraging signs we have seen, especially since the beginning of this year, mean that companies will make more profits faster, that people will go back to work
March 28, 1983

faster and be paying taxes at a faster rate than expected, perhaps the deficit will not be as high as was expected a few weeks ago.
On the week-end I read that people were now predicting that the deficit for 1983-84 might be only $24 or $25 billion instead of $30 billion. However, next fall, the Government will have to come back to Parliament for another increase in borrowing authority. Thus, if the Opposition were to cut the Government's borrowing authority by $14 billion, which is what the Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) intends to do in his amendment, it would mean that in the next financial year, there would be only about $2 billion left to conduct the Government's operations. That will not make sense at all. The Government would have to come back to the House, probably within a month or six weeks, for further borrowing authority. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South, the Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and all the Members of the Opposition who know anything about economics know perfectly well that the Government is going to be in a deficit position by June, July and August of this year, and they also realize that Parliament will have to authorize Government expenditures. If Parliament does not want to do so between now and June, July and August of this year, then it should not, so why should we waste our time and run the risk that the Government intervention on the money market will not take place in an orderly fashion? It means the Government would have to introduce another Bill in the House in April or May, instead of waiting until this fall, when another request will be necessary in any case, because the present borrowing authority will not cover more than June, July and August, since it represents about half the deficit projected for 1983-84.
Mr. Speaker, I think the Government is acting wisely by increasing its deficit in a recession, because otherwise, the full weight of the recession would fall on the people and regions that are most vulnerable in this country. Some areas are particularly sensitive to the effects of a recession, and my riding is one of them. If the Government had not decided to carry a large deficit at a time of economic recession, it would mean that those regions and those people who are particularly vulnerable in our society would carry the full weight of the recession. I think that in the present economic situation, it makes sense to use this country's financial resources to ensure that the cost of the recession to economically vulnerable individuals, groups and regions will not be as heavy and I therefore think that the Government is very sensible in taking advantage of the credit available in Canada to stimulate the economy.
Another factor we must not forget is that in a recession, although unemployment is higher than usual, there are still people working. In Canada, there are still people working and saving money. In a recession, there is a psychological reaction that makes people afraid to spend. In Canada today, 13 per cent of disposable income is invested in savings. If the Government did not intervene to borrow these funds and to reinvest them in the country in order to stimulate the economy, it
Borrowing Authority
would delay economic recovery, because today, companies and businessmen, as well as individuals, are afraid to invest. They are afraid to borrow substantial amounts of money. Therefore, if governments and not only the Federal Government but also the Provincial Governments, did not borrow this money which represents 13.5 per cent of the disposal income of Canadians today, it would be necessary to invest those savings elsewhere, outside Canada, and that would delay the recovery of the economy.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, it follows almost naturally and automatically that in a situation like this one, governments, and this includes the entire public sector, should borrow while ensuring that programs are directed towards those who are affected by the recession and at the same time, that Government action should be taken to invest in economic development, which will boost economic recovery. These funds will be borrowed to provide for continued economic activity in this country. Consumers sometimes complain that the deficit is too high in a recession. These are the people who would probably get us into a really big depression.
Mr. Speaker, that is why the Government's deficit is higher today, and I shall repeat, it is because Government revenue has dropped and certain expenditures must be maintained in the country to encourage economic recovery.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to enter this debate and to support the proposed amendment of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). Bill C-143 is the fourth major borrowing in eight months. We had Bill C- 111 in June of last year for $6.6 billion, C-125 in July, 1982 for $7 billion, C-128 in November, 1982 for $4 billion, totalling $17.6 billion in borrowing during that period. When we add Bill C-143, it totals $36.6 billion in borrowing in less than a year. This borrowing alone as proposed by the Government is in excess of $1,000 for every man, woman and child in this country.
The few Government speakers who have risen, including the Hon. Member who just finished, Mr. Speaker, have not given us any reasons why Members on the Opposition side should vote to allow the $14 billion to be borrowed without the Government putting forward a strategy, or at the very least some kind of outline of a budget.

March 28, 1983
Borrowing Authority
With respect to the $5 billion, I believe most Members of the House can glean from the Supplementary Estimates, and from the Main Estimates of the last year, some idea of what those expenditures are for. But to ask for $14 billion, however, which takes us from April 1 to October, 1983, is really quite irresponsible. The request of the Government for that kind of a blank cheque must be turned down by any Member of this House who is seriously representing his or her constituency. I heard a Liberal Member saying that we can have a look at the Main Estimates. Well, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) is here. He and I share the knowledge from our discussion of the Main Estimates that the intended expenditures of the Department of the Environment are not all included in the Main Estimates now. I believe it is irresponsible for any Member of this House to vote through a borrowing of $14 billion without expenditures being tacked down. Certainly I know that if the New Democratic Party were sitting on the Government side, there would be much howling from the Liberal Members of "Give you guys $14 billion? We don't know what you are going to do with it." And the Tories would be doing the same thing. Yet when the Members of the Liberal Party rise to speak about it, they say: "Oh, it's fine, you have the Main Estimates; you know what we are going to do".
I will point out a few things on the record, Mr. Speaker, which will give you some idea why Members on this side, both the NDP and the Conservatives, are pretty concerned about the unsound economic strategy of the Liberal Party. Tom Walkom of The Globe and Mail said just last week: "While it is not unheard of for a Government to ask for some interim borrowing authority, a $14 billion request without a budget is unprecedented". The Government would borrow $5 billion, $6 billion and $7 billion without a budget, but we are being asked for $14 billion, almost $1,000 for every man, woman and child in the country.
The question is, Mr. Speaker, can this kind of action continue, the ever-increasing borrowing, without the Government providing some detail of its intended use? Surely, what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) is proposing here is to turn Parliament into a rubberstamp for out of control Liberal pork-barrelling. Just over a year ago, Mr. Speaker, in the committee on energy matters, this same Minister, "Old ironclad", came in and asked for a $100 million write-off from Canada's taxpayers for another Liberal blunder, which was heavy water production with the Candu system. With no prospect of sales and no predicted sales, the plants are still running in full operation. In the riding of the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), they have just written off $130 million again for this year just to keep 700 jobs producing a commodity which has had no major sales in or outside of Canada in the past four years. I believe Canadians have a right to know, Mr. Speaker, that those 700 jobs are being underwritten by $200,000 a year, when in other areas of Canada, such as my riding or the riding of the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), where we have 40 per cent unemployment, all we get for various Government programs is a couple
of hundred thousand dollars. That is how much it costs to create one of these heavy water jobs, and it is what we get to provide sustenance and food on the table for thousands of people in our ridings.
We must ask, Mr. Speaker, how much hard-earned capital can be diverted into industries in some areas where Liberals try, and in some cases successfully, to obtain their places in this House through the diversion of taxpayers' money. And what about the billions of dollars owed in back taxes by the corporate sector, now roughly equal to the present deficit? Why are not the Government Members, and for that matter the Tories, clamouring for it to be paid in? Is it now so close to election time that it might jeopardize the chances of Tweedledum and Tweedledee for election donations? Why is the Minister not proposing a dramatic increase in taxes? Why shift the tax burden to the young and the unborn generations? The answer to that is quite clear: if the Minister of Finance and the Liberals were proposing to increase taxes in this country by the rate at which they are intending to borrow, and workers came home with $100 or $200 a month taken off their pay cheques, there would be chaos in this country and that Liberal Party would not be governing for very long.
Instead of doing the honest thing, which is to explain what it wants the money for, the Government is trying to go through the back door and the debt is simply going to be passed on to Canadians as yet unborn. I wonder how high a debt the Minister of Finance plans to leave as a legacy to his own children, whether $10,000, $20,000, $100,000, simply so the Liberals can continue to float what is clearly recognized in this country as an unsound economic policy. What is the money for? Is it for the Liberals to try to buy voters' confidence back? We know they are not doing it through a sophisticated industrial strategy which would decentralize the economy, encourage conservation, allow us to pursue a soft energy path now recognized by many scientists as the only way to go, which would allow us to revitalize our rural communities, put our forestry workers back to work, replant our ravaged forests or clean up our environment. Even though 75 per cent of Canadians now would support a lowering of their standard of living in order to have a cleaner environment, we see the federal Government doing very little either to clean up the Great Lakes, stop acid rain or deal with those very important matters.
Instead, Mr. Speaker, the money is going, at the rate of $800 a day, to Donald Macdonald to help write off the $100 million loss on Consolidated Computers and to continue paying the tens of millions of dollars on Mirabel Airport, when small airports, particularly in western Canada, can no longer get any money even to pave the potholes on the main runway. The money will continue to go to grants, including 80 cents on the dollar to many oil companies which already have large profits and which, as demonstrated by a report prepared by Consumer and Corporate Affairs, have ripped off consumers for hundreds of millions of dollars. Yet the Government does nothing to try to recoup that massive rip-off and try to help consumers with their cost of heating oil or gas.
March 28, 1983

What is there for home owners and renters? There have been no Government speakers who have risen and said: "There will be something for home owners and for renters". There is nothing for them, Mr. Speaker. What did the elderly get? They got it right in the neck. They got a 6 per cent and 5 per cent cut in real pension income. This is denied, of course, by Government Members, but any pensioner who takes a look at what he should be getting in terms of the present rate of inflation knows that he has been ripped off. They get nothing, Mr. Speaker, for building the country. The Liberals talk a lot but when it comes time to put cash down, the cash goes to the corporate sector.
Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, what the unborn will get in terms of just the $14 billion debt unless Members on the Government side accede to the amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South, which is a very realistic proposal and should be supported by anyone in this House who understands economics and what Parliament requires in order to vote properly on such a massive borrowing. Young Canadians will get a cut in Family Allowances. Those in schools, college, training schools and universities also get a cut, thanks to the shortsightedness of this Government's policy.
But where is the $14 billion going-setting the $5 billion aside for a moment? We need to know this, Mr. Speaker. It is irresponsible to ask for unbudgeted funds. What banker would lend anyone an amount of even $14,000, let alone $14 billion, without knowing what they are going to do with it? What federal bureaucrat, even under that Government administration, would lend or grant any money without at least some temporary guidelines? Where will the money go? It will go to corporations like the CPR in order to pay for the Prime Minister's doubletalk on double-track, while increasing by five times the cost to farmers for grain movement by 1990. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) wants to give hundreds of millions of dollars to the CPR while destroying the Crow rate. We know that only 6 per cent of Canadians are farmers now. The number is down dramatically from even ten years ago. The average age of farmers this year will creep up to the age of 60. Is it Liberal policy to turn farms in this country over to the corporate sector? We love to hear the Tories and Liberals screaming that the NDP would land bank all the property, but it is interesting to see what the right-wing strategy in terms of farming is. That is certainly what the changes to the Crow rate are.
With two million unemployed and with borrowing at $2 billion a month, I believe it would only be responsible for all Members of this House to support the amendment now proposed, which is to reduce that borrowing from $14 billion to $1 on behalf of all future generations of this country.

I would like to respond today, Mr. Speaker, specifically to the speech made by the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau). on the other side of the House, something is taken out and a cassette is put in, and what would otherwise be grossly illogical becomes parroted; and the attempt appears to be to sell that as both logic and true.
Let me refer to two specific comments made by the Hon. Member for Gloucester. His argument was that we should not be concerned about a proposal to borrow $14 billion for the next fiscal year in advance of receiving a budget because, after all, it is not for the whole year. It is not as though the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), said the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau), was trying to borrow everything he needs next year; he is only trying to borrow part of it. The fact that that in itself is a violation of Parliament's basic tradition and right does not seem to fuss him. It should as a Parliamentarian, but it does not seem to.

Mr. Speaker, I am never concerned about being heckled, I can assure you. When one is dissecting doubletalk, it is not surprising that the person who originated it in the first place wants a second kick at it.
The simple fact of the matter is this. To my knowledge, and the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) put it on the record a minute ago, no Government has ever had the audacity to come to the House of Commons and ask for anything like $14 billion without a clear budgetary statement for the year ahead.
For the sake of the Hon. Member for Gloucester I want to deal with why that breach of the traditions of Parliament is so

March 28, 1983
Borrowing Authority
important, why we oppose it, and why we support the amendment of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blen-karn). Let me remind the Hon. Member, Mr. Speaker, that last June I believe it was, or whenever Bill C-125 came before the House, when the Government's financial needs were estimated to be roughly $17 billion and it tried to borrow $21 billion, this Party fought that and the Government agreed to reduce the provision to the then known borrowing requirements. The Government agreed to a proposal made by our side that the Bill be reduced to $17 billion and that, if later the $4 billion was needed, this Party would support a limited debate on the $4 billion. That turned out to be necessary, which is not surprising because, after all, this Government's economic policy is just to keep borrowing and spending and never worry about who is going to have to pay the bill.

speechtext: There was a recession.

At the same time we were told: "You are right, we ought not to come to the House of Commons for further borrowing authority unless we have presented a budget". Now, six months later, because the Government does not dare bring in a budget, because it does not have the courage to bring in a budget, Mr. Speaker, the Government tries an end run around the traditions of 110 years of this House of Commons. That end run is this: we do not know what our budget is going to say, we do not know what our spending is going to be, we do not know what our revenue projections are going to be-

-so we will table something called the Main Estimates, which every Member of this House knows is out of whack in any given year, under this Government anywhere from 5 per cent to 15 per cent. The Government calls that its spending estimates when everyone who watches Parliament knows that is not reliable, particularly under this Government.
Then the Government invents a new tradition. It says: all we have to do to justify borrowing is table a document where we may spend, without any commitment to a budgetary document, without any debate or any of the normal ties attached to a budget vote. It is a shameful way to avoid presenting to the House of Commons the Estimates in a budget context for the next fiscal year.
That is absolutely clear to parliamentary watchers, and that is why members of the media, particularly business columnists, are so astounded. I refer again to what the Hon. Member for Skeena has read into the record from a columnist in The Globe
and Mail. That is why those analysts are so astounded, for the sake of the Hon. Member for Gloucester, Mr. Speaker, that this end run is being tried.
Let me put it, if I can, in a different context that perhaps even the Hon. Member can understand. Can he get up in his place and tell me or any Member of this House what precisely the period of time the $14 billion in borrowing-in other words, $14 billion in deficit-is to cover? Does anyone know? The answer is that nobody knows. The Minister of Finance knows full well that if he got up in this House and said: "Well, that is for the next four months", or five months, three months or six months, he would be signalling what he expects the deficit to be in budget year 1983-84. Of course he is not going to do that, because once Canadians discover precisely how bad the financial situation of this Government is, they are going to be equally astounded.
The Government has to learn two important points, Mr. Speaker. That is best exemplified by the fact that last year the Government of Canada was in the securities market for a total of 51 per cent of the net securities issued in Canada. You cannot borrow your way out of the problems we have in this country.

The Government is going to have to learn that.

In fiscal 1982-83 it comes out at 4.8 per cent of the Gross National Product, up from 2 per cent when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) first took office. Somewhere along the line the Government is going to start coming clean with Canadians, coming clean with the House, and understand and honour parliamentary traditions. subsubtopic: NEW CEREAL GRAIN TRANSPORT POLICY-MAINTENANCE OF QUEBEC BENEFITS
speechtext:
Last Saturday, in Quebec City, Madam Speaker, the Quebec wing of the General Council of the Liberal Party of Canada unanimously adopted a motion on the new grain transport policy announced on February 1.
The delegates have asked the Canadian Government that compensatory guarantees be written in the legislation so that Quebec farmers will not be unfairly treated should the equity rules in Canada be no longer respected once the new policy has been implemented. The delegates have also asked that the dairy policy be established on a lasting basis so that spokesmen for the agricultural sector will not be forced each year to make numerous representations to the Canadian Government in order that the program be maintained. The delegates also want the Livestock Feed Board of Canada to be given more extensive powers with a view to offsetting the major role of the Canadian Wheat Board in Canada.
Although the resolution dealt with many other aspects, its main purpose was to maintain the rights acquired by Quebec in a sector of the economy where, in recent years, the Canadian Government has contributed to the improvement of the situation. Some delegates expressed grave concern about the scandalous distorsion caused by Mr. Parizeau's progressive energy tax which has created a gap of tens of millions of dollars to the detriment of the overall economy of Quebec.

Madam Speaker, the representatives of the White Crow Movement, who are in the gallery today, have one purpose and one purpose only-the retention of the present statutory Crowsnest Pass freight rates. Hon. Members are being lobbied by these representatives today and tomorrow. These farmers will be seeking a simple "Yes" or "No" answer to the question of Crow retention. From the New Democratic Party they will get a unanimous "Yes" for Crow rate retention, and they will get it in Parliament and across the country in every Province.
I am certain the Conservatives will tell these representatives that they oppose the Pepin plan. But opposing Mr. Pepin will not keep the Crow. We hope our lobbyists will be seeking a clear position from each Conservative MP, because there is no provincial Conservative consensus in the West. The federal Liberal Party seems committed to Crow change, but provincial Liberal Parties in Saskatchewan and Quebec want the Crow kept and they are putting pressure on their Members here.
These citizens with the White Crow Movement have come 2,000 miles to tell us how the loss of the Crow rate will affect them as farmers, members of communities, and as producers in the larger Canadian economy.
Their message is a compelling one. The New Democratic Party position is clear. We would keep the Crow. I trust all Members will give the White Crow people a thorough hearing.

Madam Speaker, the Drumheller Institution was built to handle a maximum of 400 prisoners; it now houses 560 inmates.
The Institution was widely advertised when it was built as medium security, to house young offenders. Its population now includes inmates of all ages, and about half of the prisoners should be in a maximum security institution.
The Drumheller Institution has no segregation cells and, with little work available, most of the prisoners are in the open room at the same time. This, along with double bunking in seven foot by nine foot cells, and insufficient places for the inmates to eat, creates an inflammatory situation. As a result, young offenders who are serving their first sentence for nonviolent acts that forced no one else to do anything wrong, and who are not really criminals at all, who realize that they made a mistake and want to put that behind them and start a new life, are now being harassed by older inmates to a point that is hardly bearable. This situation is most unfair and is certainly doing nothing to rehabilitate the young offenders. It is actually breeding criminals.
I call on the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) to commence at once to move the maximum security type prisoners to a maximum security institution where there are facilities to handle them, and to grant early parole to first-time offenders who committed non-violent mistakes.
The situation is so tense now that we could have another Archambault if action is not taken.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to make a statement pursuant to Standing Order 21 regarding an issue that is very important to many in my constituency of Parkdale-High Park.
The Ukrainian Canadian Committee has named this Yuri Shukhevych Week-a week hat has come to mean a great deal for the Ukrainian people. Yuri was first arrested in 1948, at

March 28, 1983
the age of 14, and sentenced to ten years of imprisonment in Vladimir Prison, for being the son of Roman Shukhevych, the Commander in Chief of the Ukrainian Partisan Army (UPA). By the end of his prison term in March of 1987, Shukhevych will have spent 35 years in prison and exile. Hence, he has come to represent much more to the Ukrainian people than simply another dissident in a concentration camp; he has come to represent their aspirations for a free Ukraine.
It is fitting that we remeber Yuri today, for today is his birthday.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. These statements should not be used for congratulating or commemorating someone. I understand the Hon. Member's feelings, but unless he has a statement to make on a particular issue, I cannot accept his statement.

speechtext: As Chairman of the Canadian Parliamentary Helsinki Group, I urge the Department of External Affairs to make representations to the Soviet Union Government, through the appropriate channels, for the immediate release of Yuri Shukhevych and others who find themselves in a similar predicament.

Madam Speaker, last week the Court of Appeal of Alberta reduced the sentence of a man convicted of rape, from eight years to four years, for reasons that must be abhorrent to all decent pepole, and especially this Parliament which recently passed amendments on sexual assault.
The victim of the sexual assault is crippled by polio, has braces on her legs, and uses a crutch. She met her assailant, a former neighbour, in a bar, and went back to his apartment for beer and marijuana. Surely we should not have to explain that accepting the invitation to a legal beer or illegal marijuana does not imply acceptance of sexual assault.
The judgment states that "sexual intercourse took place after a short time", but the better word is assault, for, as the judgment notes, "the jury found that it was without her consent and violence was used". The accused was, at that time, serving a three-year sentence for a previous rape.
According to the original trial judge, "Eve sat on the bench for ten years, and the circumstances of this crime, I can say, without exception, are the worst I've ever seen."
A four year sentence is not inconsequential, but we must take exception to the reasoning, to wit: "We think the circumstances are such that it would not have been surprising to that young woman that something might well happen to her going up to the man's apartment between two and three o'clock in the morning-"
The courts must learn that "No" means "No" at two o'clock in the morning, three o'clock, or high noon.

Madam Speaker, the Government seems to be losing sight of the perspective that society must be protected against anti-social behaviour and those convicted of it; that the public, too, has rights, along with convicted felons; that the penalty for crime is punishment; and that, even though we temper punishment with compassion and mercy, we must accept the fact that certain cases are above redemption and rehabilitation.
In Vancouver this weekend a convicted rapist, described by the Chief Justice of British Columbia as "a menace to society", has been set free by a court when it ruled the Parole Board acted illegally by arresting him upon his release on mandatory supervision. The B.C. Chief Justice also said "the liberty of the subject has to be waived in juxtaposition to the safety of the public at large."
I realize that the Supreme Court of Canada is dealing with the issue on May 17, but I just want to put the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) on notice that Canadians have had their fill of animals being returned to society to strike again.

subtopic: FUTURE OF "REACH FOR THE TOP" PROGRAM
FUTURE OF "REACH FOR THE TOP" PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to call attention to the fact that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation may cancel one of its better programs, "Reach for the Top". The Canadian content of this program is 100 per cent. It features outstanding Canadian students-intellectual stars at the teenage level.
Everyone agrees that our most precious Canadian resource is our young people. I am certain that all Canadians want "Reach for the Top" to continue. Let us hope they will write to the CBC and let it know. As Members of Parliament, let us see that the CBC gets the message when we are studying the estimates.
We suggest that this program be continued. We are advised, however, that both regional and network program directors made a recommendation that the series be cancelled. They gave the reason as "not reaching the intended target audience". I would suggest that all that is required is a little imagination-a change of format and possibly more play-offs, more short-term competition. Surely the minds at the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation can find a way to save this all Canadian, young peoples' show.
March 28, 1983

Madam Speaker, today in Montreal a matter involving RCMP Corporal Zephreim Fortin is being heard by the Federal Court.
The issue is an important one for many RCMP members, involving the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which seems to be violated by the discharge or retirement procedures of the RCMP which, coincidentally, were changed last Thursday by administrative bulletin AM536. Very briefly, the issue which is being joined by a writ of prohibition by counsel for Corporal Fortin, involves the existing practice of retiring RCMP members at a lower age level if they have a lower rank, or perhaps to put it differently, on the basis of rank rather than ability.
On October 20, last year, the Commissioner of Human Rights, Mr. Fairweather, expressed his views on this procedure in the case of Sergeant Entwhistle of Fredericton, New Brunswick. However, the problem of differing ages for differing ranks regarding their length of service continues to upset members.
I ask the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) to review this general practice even though the relevant section of the Charter of Rights will not be operative until 1985. It does represent an obvious and contining injustice and concerns the service representatives and the members of the Association of 17 Divisions who are looking for changes in this manifestly unfair practice.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):

subtopic: CANADIAN EQUIPMENT ON NEWLY LAUNCHED SATELLITE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to inform this House that scientists at the Department of National Defence, Department of Communications, and at Spar Aerospace Limited, have successfully launched a satellite today to be used in search and rescue operations in Canada. Canadian designed equipment was launched today at about 11 o'clock our time aboard a U.S. weather satellite from Vandenburg Air Force Base in California. This search and rescue equipped satellite joins two similar Soviet satellites, the first of which has already contributed to the successful rescue of 17 North Americans.
This important addition to Canadian search and rescue capabilities is part of an international experimental program in which Canada has been a leading member along with the United States, France, and the Soviet Union. As well as saving lives, this satellite system should also reduce the risk to search and rescue forces who often operate under severe and dangerous conditions.
By participating in this high technology program Canadian industry will continue to remain in the forefront of this sector of space technology.
This successful launch today marks another important milestone for Canada in a very important, humanitarian program, and enhances internationally our already well established capabilities in space communications research and development. It also underlines the Government's commitment to improve search and rescue services continuously by every means possible, for all Canadians.
The issue in question is the justification of spending-
