subtopic: FINANCIAL PLIGHT OF FARMERS-REQUEST THAT BANKS SHOW TOLERANCE
FINANCIAL PLIGHT OF FARMERS-REQUEST THAT BANKS SHOW TOLERANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I take this opportunity to remind Hon. Members that the House has unanimously agreed to expedite Bill C-653, an Act, to amend the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. I take also this opportunity to remind lending institutions which are at times rather over-anxious to be paid back that Parliament has acted unanimously. Tomorrow, the committee will start sitting again; beginning April the 11th, it will hold public hearings and will hear witnesses who will make representations concerning ways and means to avert a great many farm bankruptcies.
I simply raise this issue to urge lending institutions to show a little more understanding toward our farmers who may have fallen back in their payments, for they are perfectly aware that Parliament will accept unanimously, as it did in the case of Bill C-653, any recommendation aimed at preventing the bankruptcies of several farmers.

Madam Speaker, on May 1 the hundreds of lay-offs which the CNR announced last January will be taking effect. I would like to take this opportunity to encourage the Minister of Transport and the Government to prevail upon the CNR to cancel these lay-offs.
We all know that when the economic recovery comes we will need a railroad and the equipment, and if we do not put these people to work now, three years hence the railways will be whining and snivelling that they do not have their equipment

March 28, 1983
Oral Questions
ready and in place. The railroads are now laying people off for short-term budgetary reasons when there is work waiting to be done. Hundreds of people will be laid off on May 1 if the Government does not lean on the CNR to change its mind.
The railways led many people to believe that the lay-offs were related to the Crow and that they needed changes in the Crow rate. Now we have propsals made by the Government to change the Crow, and yet the lay-offs are to go ahead. If the railroads want to bargain in good faith with the Canadian people they ought to cancel the lay-offs for May 1, and, of course, at the same time accept the NDP proposal to keep the Crow, a proposal which would give them the same amount of money but would keep more people at work and solve many problems which the Pepin-Gilson proposal does not solve.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR MEASURES TO STIMULATE JOB CREATION
speechtext:
I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Finance, Madam Speaker. The Conference Board in Canada is today estimating that, if you add the discouraged workers to the 1.6 million unemployed reported for February, we would have a real unemployment rate in Canada of 19 per cent as opposed to 12.5 per cent.
This prompts me to ask the Minister of Finance, given that range of unemployment unprecedented in our country why is he not bringing in measures to stimulate employment now rather than waiting until the budget? The Minister knows that when he does bring in the budget with these stimulative measures there will still be a substantial time lag, which means the situation will get worse. Why does the Minister not bring in these measures now?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR MEASURES TO STIMULATE JOB CREATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am advised the Conference Board estimate is to the effect that, had it counted discouraged workers, the unemployment figure would rise by 6 per cent or 7 per cent, but it is 6 per cent or 7 per cent of 1.5 million, not 6 per cent over and above 12 per cent. Therefore, the Hon. Member's mathematics are not fairly representing the point of view of the Conference Board. Be that as it may, the number of unemployed is indeed very high and if we include the discouraged workers it would certainly add to the total number.
I indicated to the Leader of the NDP on Friday that we already have $2 billion worth of direct job and indirect job stimulation at the present time in the economy.
The Senate is now considering the Income Tax Act. I hope this Bill will be passed before Wednesday, at which time we
will be able to send refunds to Canadians, meaning that over the next two months some S6.5 billion will be injected into the economy in direct money that Canadians can spend. As I indicated, I expect to be able to bring forward the budget reasonably soon after we return in April.
I think the adoption of the Income Tax Act and the programs already in effect will play a significant role at least in alleviating the difficulties which many, many Canadians are facing at the present time.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR MEASURES TO STIMULATE JOB CREATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I doubt whether any of the 2 million unemployed, certainly the discouraged workers, the long-time unemployed workers in this country, can look forward to any tax refunds. That measure is a matter of complete indifference to them.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: ESTIMATED COST OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of Finance. I can cite economists who are predicting that unemployment payments could rise to $12.3 billion this year from $8.6 billion in 1982. Could the Minister confirm that this is a correct estimate? Could he also tell the House whether it is his intention to bring in a further increase in unemployment premiums in addition to the 40 per cent increase in premiums last year which, in itself, is a disincentive to creating jobs in the private sector?

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member is asking me to confirm some predictions made by a private organization. I already indicated I was not going to spend my time discussing predictions from various institutions, for the simple reason that such predictions change constantly.
As far as our own predictions are concerned regarding the Unemployment Insurance Fund deficit for next year, I myself or some of my colleagues will be dealing with this matter during the budget debate. I do not know whether my hon. colleague would or would not want us to increase unemployment insurance premiums but whatever his position is, namely, whether he is prepared to see the Unemployment Insurance Fund deficit increase or whether he wants us to bring that deficit down, I should be happy to hear his views and consider them in the light of the budget.
I can inform the Hon. Member right away that as far as we are concerned, we are not now considering an increase in unemployment insurance premiums.
March 28, 1983

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING DATE OF BUDGET PRESENTATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister knows full well that another increase in unemployment insurance premiums over and above the 40 per cent last year would be a disincentive to job creation in the private sector.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: DETERMINATION OF BENEFITS BASED ON RESIDENCE FACTOR
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I explained to the Hon. Member at the time, we have divided the country into 40 regions under the unemployment insurance system. When you do that division, you have to draw the boundaries somewhere. Usually they are drawn according to the longer term historical pattern of the unemployment rate because, as the Hon. Member knows, we have to gauge the various entrants requirements and other qualifying requirements according to those longer term trends. It is quite true that, during this time of recession, the area of Burlington has experienced more severe unemployment, but generally it has been a high employment area with a very stable workforce.
As I indicated at that time, all of the boundaries are under review. We cannot make one boundary change because, once you make one, it has a domino effect and affects every other boundary in a region. Therefore, they have to be balanced out. We are trying to look at what the longer term trends will be and adjust them, if adjustments are necessary, according to those trends, not simply responding to the short term circumstances that we are now experiencing.

subsubtopic: PENALTIES IMPOSED FOR RENEGOTIATION OF MORTGAGES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Several of my constituents have found themselves in a closed mortgage situation where they are paying 18'A per cent, and I believe all Hon. Members will find this is a typical situation. When they try to open these mortgages they are told they have to pay a three-month penalty. I believe most right thinking Canadians are prepared to accept that. Unfortunately, the trust companies and the banks are now saying that they want something in addition to that amount, as much as $7,000 on a $40,000 mortgage. Is the Minister of Finance prepared to direct the

presidents of the trust companies and the banks, or meet with them and ask them if they could accept their social responsibility? They have made 1814 per cent for two years on these mortgages. That is a handsome profit. It is time they limited themselves to a three-month interest penalty.

subsubtopic: FRENCH ISLANDS-NEGOTIATION OF MARITIME BOUNDARIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and has to do with the relations between Canada and France. Can the Minister give us any indication of the progress being made, if there is any progress, in negotiations relating to the maritime boundaries around Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FRENCH ISLANDS-NEGOTIATION OF MARITIME BOUNDARIES
speechtext: Yes, Madam Speaker, several weeks ago there was a further meeting between Canadian and French officials at which both the boundaries and the fishing problems were discussed. The Canadian side has asked for a period of further examination before resuming these negotiations. Just recently there was a communication from the Government of France, which we are presently considering. It is not apparent to us at the moment that Canadian interests would be advanced by an immediate resumption of negotiations, but we are considering the matter.

Madam Speaker, is the Minister suggesting there is a linkage between the fishing rights of the French fishermen in the area and the 200 mile limit territorial boundary negotiations? If he is, can he say now whether he feels it can be done on a bilateral basis or whether it is going to have to go to the International Court the way our boundary disputes with the United States have gone?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am not drawing a link between the nature of the settlement of the international boundary and, for example, the ability or willingness of Canada to provide quotas to the French fleet now or in the future, especially when the moment comes that the French fleet loses its fishing possibilities in the Gulf. There is a link, however, operationally in how enforcement might be undertaken. There has been an understanding between the two Governments as to how enforcement will take place in disputed areas.
Finally, with regard to the last question, it would not be my desire to search for a way to bring this matter to the International Court. As the Hon. Member knows, we have a very massive case there presently, affecting the Atlantic coast, and it would not be my wish to add to that.

Has the Bureau participated in foreign projects during each of the past three years and, if so (a) how many (b) what was the total dollar value (c) how many man-years were involved by the Bureau (d) in how many of the projects were management consultants from the private sector eligible to compete with the Bureau for the work?

subsubtopic: BUREAU OF MANAGEMENT CONSULTING
speechtext:
1 and 2.
The Bureau of Management Consulting employs 110 professional persons in Ottawa. The Bureau's participating in foreign projects during the past three years is as follows:
Year	Number of Projects	Dollar Value	Person YearsFY 80/81	5	$176,150	1.2FY 81/82	10	$425,500	4.6FY 82/83	9	$471,000	4.7
The Bureau offers an optional service to Canadian Government Departments and, through External Affairs and the Canadian Commercial Corporation, to foreign governments and international agencies. Since the service is optional, clients always have the freedom to offer their consulting assignments to private sector consultants. If the Canadian private sector is invited to bid, the Bureau, as a matter of policy, will either not compete or will withdraw if a proposal has already been made.
In the foreign projects noted above, the Bureau was approached by the various agencies on the basis of their perception that the Bureau had the expertise to solve the problem. They had already decided not to use the Canadian private sector and to negotiate a government/international agency to government contract. In fact, on the 24 foreign assignments during the years 1980/81 to 1982/83, the Bureau used, on a sub-contract basis, 15 consultants from the Canadian private sector.

speechtext:
Returning to the concern of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South regarding the attitude of the present Government toward the wishes of the Canadian people, it is quite clear that Canadians are feeling more and more that the present Government has not shown a willingness to listen to them. As we debate Bill C-143 today, I note that this Wednesday marks the sixth week that the Bill has been before the House. Many of us in the Opposition have spoken more than once on this Bill precisely because we feel the Canadian people, and ourselves, need to be listened to by this Government.
This Government is asking for a sum of money that we think is unreasonable: it is asking for $19 billion. Most of us accept the fact that it may be necessary to give the Government $5 billion, which is needed for this present fiscal year; but most of us have reservations about the need for us to give the Government authority to borrow another $14 billion on top of that.
I had occasion to speak on this Bill some three and a half weeks ago. At that time I chose to comment mainly about some of my perceptions and views regarding the present Government. I was concerned about some of the characteristics that have been exhibited over the last several years in this House. I mentioned the deplorable characteristic of this Government's untrustworthiness. As I mentioned, that applies to the attitude concerning Bill C-143.
We had been told previously by two cabinet Ministers that we would not be given this kind of borrowing Bill until we
were told more about how the money would be spent. In the Government's untrustworthy manner, this has not taken place and it is most regrettable. In spite of the many demands from this side of the House, we are still not being given any information as to how this $14 billion will be spent.
When I spoke on March 4, I indicated that I was concerned about the characteristics of arrogance and secrecy and the general contempt the Government has shown for Parliament in general. That observation could be a speech in itself. There are many ways in which we can see how this present Government really does not trust Parliament and does not want to see Parliament functioning.
That brings me to a point on which I want to elaborate today. I do not pretend to be a student of parliamentary government although I am very fascinated and interested in it. If what I say is wrong, I would like to be corrected by some Hon. Member. My perception of the parliamentary system is that the Government is there to govern. There is a real role for the Opposition as well, particularly the Official Opposition. The Opposition is given certain defined terms of reference, one might say. The Opposition is there to protect the public from the tyranny of a majority Government, and to protect the public in particular against the unwise use of their money. I sense more and more that the present Government is showing that kind of disrespect to which I have just alluded. This Government is refusing to accept the fact that the Opposition Party has a real role to play in holding up this kind of unnecessary and costly type of legislation to spend the taxpayers's dollars. Since the Government has known for the last six weeks that Members on this side of the House were concerned about how the Government would spend the taxpayers' money, there is no reason why it could not have made an amendment or change to the borrowing authority Bill.
Let us review what the Government actually said when it presented the Bill on February 16. We received a press release from the Department of Finance which explained that the first part of the Bill asked for authorization to borrow $5 billion for the immediate fiscal year, and the second part of the Bill asked for $14 billion for the next fiscal year beginning in April, at the end of this week.
The reason given for asking for this borrowing authority was that the Government was unable to anticipate the drop in revenues which occurred and the increased debt charges. It said that those two phenomena, the decrease of revenue and the increase in debt charges, accounted for 72 per cent of its problems. The other 28 per cent accounted for "recession related expenditures". It referred to the rising cost of Unemployment Insurance. While that increase is understandable, the press release did not mention the other increases involved in that 28 per cent. I did not mention spending $1.5 billion for Petro-Canada to buy Petrofina. It did not mention the $800 a day being paid to Donald Macdonald which we have heard so much about. We were not told about those shady deals, in my

view, for which they have to borrow money from the Canadian people.
Before I discuss the details of the Government's request for the extra $14 billion, let me talk about the Government's inability to predict what its needs will be. On November 18, 16 months ago, the official prediction for our deficit was $10.5 billion. In June of last year, which is less than a year ago, the Government predicted that deficit would be up to $19.6 billion, which has almost doubled in seven months. As of October of last year the prediction had gone up to $23.6 billion. As recently as last month the prediction went up to $27.2 billion. In approximately 16 months, the deficit had risen by at least two and one-half times from what the Government had anticipated. That is the incompetence Canadians are faced with from the Government.
When such lack of competence in a Government is evident, it is no wonder that the Opposition becomes worried and feels the responsibility to put pressure on the Government to give a better explanation of its operations.
I would like to take a couple of more moments to elaborate on the statement made by the office of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). The press release stated that one reason the Government had to bring in this borrowing authority Bill was in order to permit the Government to continue with an orderly debt program. I become concerned when the Government talks about an orderly debt program because I am not in favour of debt programs at all. I believe that we should avoid having some of these debt programs. If this is an orderly debt program, I would hate to see what a disorderly debt program would be like if we did hot have this particular Bill.
Another interesting fact which evolved from the Minister's news release was that this interim authority was meant to give Parliament adequate time to consider a new borrowing Bill based on the financial requirements for 1983-84 that would be set out in the forthcoming budget. It is the intention of the Government to introduce such a Bill shortly after the next budget.
If the budget is to come down in April, the Bill would likely be introduced some time in May, which is reasonable. If we are to see the next borrowing authority Bill introduced shortly after the budget in April, surely it would be reasonable for the House to authorize borrowing for the months of April, May and possibly June, which would represent about a quarter of the year's deficit. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome the opportunity to speak to this Bill today. The legislation before the House consists of two flimsy pages with few words on them. It is not a heck of a lot to present to the House of Commons when seeking to borrow $19 billion. That is why Members on this side of the House have demanded from the Government a rational explanation of what it intends to do with these borrowed funds. That is a legitimate request. The Government should have responded to it before coming to the House asking for this borrowing authority. We should have had a budget for a request for this vast sum of money.
The important point in the debate is why the Government is in need of such a large sum of money. Fundamentally, it comes down to the fact that the Government has been mismanaging the economy, putting its economic focus in the wrong place. Therefore, we have an economic slowdown and record high levels of unemployment, which obviously means the Government revenues drop and the need of the Government to borrow increases dramatically. That is why the Government is seeking unheard levels of borrowing on such flimsy information.
When it comes to economic policies, the priorities of this Government are out of whack. Government emphasis has been on inflation. The six and five program was intended to bring down inflation. What it did was to reduce the amount of
money in people's pockets, and, therefore, reduce their purchasing power. It reduced the demand in the economy and served as a further break on economic activity. It contributed to the drop in revenues from which the Government is presently suffering. It added to the need to borrow the large sum of money for which the Government is now seeking authority. The request of the Government to borrow $19 billion is really an admission of the failure of its economic policies. It is a clear indication of the need for an alternative set of economic priorities and economic policies. This includes not only the whole question of how the Government should intervene in the economy, but also includes the whole matter of tax reform, in other words, how the Government would raise revenue. Obviously, if a Government is running a deficit, it must have something to do with how it is raising its funds as well.
I would like to make a few central points, Mr. Speaker. The first point is the fact that the present recession in terms of economic activity in this country, and, certainly, depression in terms of unemployment, really points to a long overdue need for a real industrial strategy, some intelligent thinking and action about where private and public investment in this country is going to go. We need an industrial strategy in order to ensure that we have a strong economy and one that can produce jobs, which in turn would produce revenue for the Government, thereby reducing the need for the large kinds of borrowing which the Government is proposing today. We need an industrial strategy which is based on the principle that the public has a right to have some say about what kind of investments are going to be made within the country and what kind of economic activity is going to make sense, not only in terms of profit, but also in terms of employment, and it is through the Government that the general citizenry of the country has a chance to have some say about the economic direction of the country.
In spite of this obvious need for an industrial strategy, the Government has been backing away from Government intervention in the economy. It is starting to echo the Conservatives in terms of their "hands-off' economic philosophy, in other words, to leave the direction of the economy to the private sector in the hope that somehow the private businessmen all by themselves will know better how to manage the economy, how to create wealth and how to provide employment.
The experience which we have had in this country with that philosophy and that approach has been dismal, Mr. Speaker. It is really on the basis of that philosophy of leaving the fundamental management of the economy to the private sector that we have arrived at the present economic morass in which we find ourselves today. Also it is as a result of the application of this philosophy in the United States that we are suffering from our present economic difficulties. President Reagan was elected on the basis of a philosophy which said there was really no place in economic matters for the Government or for the public, and with this philosophy he reduced public spending and Government intervention in the economy which resulted in

March 28, 1983

the predictable world-wide recession from which we are suffering today.
I must remind the House, Mr. Speaker, of the extent of our economic suffering. We cannot forget the fact that we have some 1.5 million people officially unemployed in this country and, obviously, every unemployed person reduces the revenues which can go to the Government because they are no longer in a position to pay taxes. We have 1.5 million people unemployed, but we have to add to that number those people who have just given up looking for work because they just cannot find any. They have become discouraged and given up. On top of that we have to add those people working part-time and those who are not working at full capacity because they cannot find the kind of employment they are qualified for. When you add those people in, you find the real level of unemployment in this country to be over a couple of million people. It has been reported that the real unemployment rate in this country is actually something like 19 per cent rather than the official rate of around 12 per cent.
The fact that the Government is before us today, Mr. Speaker, asking for record borrowing authority of $19 million should not be any surprise because the Government has been putting emphasis on bringing down inflation-at least, has been taking credit for bringing down inflation-and has been ignoring the need for job creation in any significant way. It has not put the necessary priority on employment. And when I say "priority on employment", what I am talking about is the fact that a humane society, as was pointed out by the Bishops not too long ago, really has to adopt the objective of full employment. In other words, every person who is capable of working and desires to work has the right to work. It is just not good enough to run the economy in a way that leaves a couple of million people out of work. By running the economy in that way, the Government is left with reduced revenues and, therefore, with a larger deficit. What the Government is saying by its actions is that it prefers to have people on welfare and on unemployment insurance benefits, rather than employed, creating wealth and engaging in productive and fulfilling activities.
It is a well-known fact in this country, Mr. Speaker, that over the last few decades the burden of taxes in this country has fallen more and more heavily on the individual rather than the corporation, and that the income tax in this country is no longer progressive; for example, those who earn more do not necessarily pay more taxes. In order to supply revenue to the Government so that it can do those things it needs to have done such as job-creation programs, there must be a decent and fair corporate and income tax system.

The Departments which were sloppy and over-allocated did not mind losing some. In any event, we then saw another progression toward accountability when we had the Comptroller General, Mr. Harry Rogers, appointed upon the presentation of the report of Mr. Lambert's commission. I think our late colleague, Bob Andras, subscribed to this kind of fiscal and financial accountability. The Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) has certainly contributed a great deal toward bringing forward in the public consciousness the sort of value for money, special procedures and cost effectiveness concepts, which finally, I believe, are bringing some financial accountability to this Chamber.

Surely it is almost an absurdity that the Government is reduced to this kind of shortterm and obvious hand-to-mouth financing when it comes to running the affairs of our country.
Now, Sir, there is obviously a great responsibility on all Members of Parliament to make sure that the Government, when it is considering accountability and the spending of such vast amounts of money, pay greater attention to ongoing programs. Right now in the Department of Public Works the Minister has to grapple with the effects of the mortgage management portfolio system which has turned out to be a horror show, but which he inherited. It has wasted tens of millions of dollars of taxpayers' money. There are also indications that the Auditor General, Mr. Dye, is going to take
another extraordinarily practical step in combating this kind of waste, as well as the item like the $100 million or $200 million, I forget which, overspending in the Montreal postal terminal debacle, which the Minister of the day denied even existed when I asked him about it. Obviously the Auditor General will have to institute an ongoing audit for large capital projects so that when he sees these kinds of excesses, based on political or other reasons, which are causing taxpayers to be ripped off for millions, he will have the authority to step in and give a little bit of guidance, or at least demand some explanations. In the past, Auditors General have had to wait until literally the horse was stolen before they went into the barn and announced the bad news to the taxpayers. Now, perhaps, if these trends can be carried on which the late Mr. Macdonell instituted and which Mr. Dye appears to be consolidating and expanding, we can get a more selective, astute and efficient spending of the hundreds of millions of dollars that many Departments waste each year.
Just to show you, Mr. Speaker, how the Government has grown, I think it was Peter Newman in Maclean's Magazine last summer who indicated that Sir John A. Macdonald had approximately 12 or 13 Cabinet Ministers and about 300 civil servants. Today each of the 36 Ministers in this administration, if you average it out, have approximately 17,000 civil servants under their administration. That is a tremendous increase. While it is unrealistic to advocate wholesale cuts in the Public Service, and I certainly do not, I think it is realistic to advocate a more selective approach to the use of consultants, a practice which costs the country hundreds of millions of dollars every year and in many cases only supplements or bolsters the expertise of many civil servants whom we are already paying very well for doing the same job which apparently has to be sanctioned again by consultants who are usually more notable for what they have done in the past for the Party in power than any great expertise they bring to the
I for one, Mr. Speaker, would not advocate delaying this measure any more. For the reasons mentioned, 1 think the Government needs the money. I hope that in the future it will use it more judiciously than it has in the past. I hope we can expect the same degree of conscientiousness from the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) we now have, that has existed in some of the recent Ministers in the job. I hope the Government will seriously consider searching for some new sources of revenue, such as the Maritimes Pollution Claims Fund, and as well will consider changing some of the tax provisions which are counterproductive. Certainly nothing so stultified the industry, ingenuity and ambition of Canadians as the imposition of the capital gains tax which this Government brought it in years ago. At the present time the continuing existence of this tax, unindexed, only fosters confiscation by the state of property that people have accumulated and which has only increased in value because of inflation, but is taxed, none the less. I see you are indicating my time has expired, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 28, I spoke on this Bill and one of the amendments before us at that time. Now, a month later, I come back to the same subject again. Like the Hon. Member who has just spoken, I am going to try to be constructive, if I can, in helping the Government consider different ways of getting out of the trouble it is in. I suspect the Government already knows these ideas are worthy of consideration. For instance, in my speech a month ago I suggested two ideas they could look at to be put into committee. One was that we should use the Bank of Canada to help us get over this pressure we are under now with this present Bill which calls for the borrowing of a total of $19 billion. Now, I did not hear any comments in the press about these proposals, and I am used to that, so I am going to make them again. What did I mean by using the Bank of Canada? Well, if you read the Bank of Canada Act, which is 50 years old, you will realize that it was put in at a time when Canada was in terrible trouble on fiscal and monetary policy. We were at the beginning of what turned out to be a Depression of nearly ten years. The Government set up the Bank of Canada, took away from the commercial banks the power to control the money supply and gave it to the central Bank. For long periods in the Depression the Governments under Bennett and Mackenzie King, quietly used the Bank of Canada to pay the costs of operating the Government because they were not collecting the taxes. At that time there were so many people unemployed and there was so much unused plant capacity that there was no inflation. In the view of many people, we are not far from that situation today, Mr. Speaker.
A month ago I suggested that we use the Bank of Canada, and then just last week I heard that the Government is using emergency power. I assume that these emergency powers are the Governor General's warrants approach. I do not know the final answer, although I will eventually find it, but I wonder if the Government is not using the key to this type of approach. Certainly, the purpose of the Governor General's warrants is to carry the Government in an emergency such as when an election is called before the money has been voted. That is almost the situation today. The Act makes it very clear that no interest is paid to the Bank of Canada in that case. One of the heaviest loads that any Government carries today is the cost of interest at the present high rates.
1 put that forward at this late stage of the debate and ask Members of the Government who are present to find out if the Bank of Canada is being used. If that is the case and there have been no evil results, then perhaps we should follow the precedents of Bennett and King and use it more. I do not think that would cause inflation if there is a labour supply, unused plant capacity and, above all, a not too fast circulation of money. The velocity of money flow is not included in our monetary activities at the present time, although I think it should be.
Perhaps the Government has stumbled on something that is in harmony with what I said a month ago. It certainly should consider this matter again because it may do a great deal of
Borrowing Authority
harm if it tries to borrow $19 billion on the market in the next few months. That could create the impression in the minds of business people and investors that we are about to enter another inflationary period. In that case, interest rates would rise immediately and undo the achievement of the declining interest rates of the last six months.
I should like to suggest that the Government ask those who have the power to inquire, whether this technique of using the Bank of Canada is being followed. The trick is to do it quietly and get over the situation of having to borrow $19 billion at high rates.
The other proposal that I made a month ago was that the Government not borrow at rates of 10, 11 or 12 per cent but at about 3 per cent. That is all that money is worth. People will lend it at that rate if they have a guarantee that if there is inflation this year-and there will be some-the interest at the end of the year will be indexed for the year. But the principal will also be indexed, to keep its real value. If an investor of the type who puts his money in Government bonds as a rule, wants to lend money at 3 per cent, he just wants to be sure that he will get it back without any loss in value. This idea probably sounds kooky, but it should be tried to see what happens.
I suggest it would not give the impression that a lot of inflation is expected. If $19 billion is borrowed at an interest rate of 10, 11 or 12 per cent for three or four months, then the country may be forced back into the recession from which we are just emerging.
In the last two or three years, the basic problem of any government in any country has been getting interest rates down. I repudiate those monetarists who suggest that interest rates are the tool to control the economy of the country and the external value of our dollar. Let the markets decide those things. We should quit fooling around with fine tuning. I think that getting interest rates down would be accepted by everyone. Even the lenders of money know that if they destroy their customers they destroy themselves.
There are several things the Government could move on, Mr. Speaker. Let us put the old Farm Credit Corporation back to the terms that existed in 1933. In statutory form, the maximum interest rate under the Farm Credit Corporation was 5 per cent, and it was given power to lend 20 times the amount of capital. The same thing could apply to small business, to export business, and so on. We could move on that.
There are other ways of achieving this, such as through the principle of the Small Business Development Bond, as suggested in the Crosbie budget. This could be applied without cost but would give a tremendous impetus to business without altering the ways and means of the budget.
Finally, the mining industry, the energy industry and the forest industry have taken a terrible beating in the last few years. We must face the fact that what is set out in the Government's reports is correct. There will never be another low-grade mine developed in Canada, the reports say, under our present tax structure where two Governments are gouging the

March 28, 1983
Borrowing Authority
industry. I think we must revert to the way things were done in the mining industry years ago. Because it was a capital intensive, high-risk operation, no taxes were paid until the debts were paid off. There was a three-year holiday. Today, instead of the three-year proviso, I would stipulate no taxes until the debts are paid off. There would be enough money left for both levels of Government and to give a return on capital and make the risk worthwhile to the mining entrepreneurs.
The same principle should be applied to energy companies. They are highly capitalized and have a long pay-out period so they cannot operate at present interest rates. They were not even operating very well when interest rates were 4 or 6 per cent. High-risk, low grade propositions such as natural gas, heavy oils, tar sands and so on, should be subject to the same rule as is applied to the mining industry-the Government gets off their backs until debts are paid off. The volume of business would mean that there would be something for everyone even at a low rate of tax.
That is all I wanted to say, Mr. Speaker. These are some simple proposals that can be considered although some of them may be thought to be kooky. At times like this, however, we had better consider every type of scenario.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in report stage debate of Bill C-143, the borrowing authority Bill. I have only been in the House of Commons for four years but in the last year I feel that all we have debated is borrowing Bills. This is the fourth one this year, and there have been seven or eight in the whole session, so we have spent a considerable amount of time talking about borrowing money.
This year the Government will borrow $26.2 billion, and I am sure it will be back next year asking for authority to borrow more money, even though the $14 billion requested in this Bill will take it into next year.
This is the largest borrowing Bill in the history of Canada. The figures do not mean too much to the Canadian people because no one can relate to $19 billion. Take a look at the remarks which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) made in the debate on second reading of this Bill. He said:
This Bill is one in a series of necessary steps being taken to deal with the extremely difficult economic situation facing this country.
When you take a look at a statement like that and you realize who has been running the country for the last number of years, and you realize that not only has there been deficit financing every year, in good times and bad, but also increases in the deficit from time to time, then you understand the hollowness of that statement. Another statement of the Minister's is as follows:
-I want to emphasize that financial requirements have risen because of unexpectedly harsh cyclical forces. The Government of Canada remains committed to its longer term goal of systematic restraint of its expenditures as a proportion of the GNP, and to systematic reduction of the deficit as well.
Let me read that last little phrase again:
-and to systematic reduction of the deficit as well.
We have seen no evidence of that in the last decade and prior to that. There has, however, been one exception. That exception was the budget brought in by the Clark Government in 1979. It laid out very clearly the method of reducing the deficit over a period of five years and beyond. The one and only time this was done over the last number of years was done by a Progressive Conservative Government. For the Minister of Finance to say that he is dedicated "to systematic reduction of the deficit as well" is a very hollow statement indeed. We can take those words, I think, very lightly, because there has been no proof of it from the other side.
The spending of this Government over the last 15 years is staggering. It is very difficult even for a Member of Parliament to grasp the tremendous increase in spending around here. The Liberals do very interesting things. I can give an example of what has been done right in my own constituency of Brampton-Georgetown. This Government in its wisdom has decided to move the Citizenship Court from the regional seat of Brampton where it has been located since 1976 to Mississauga. Prior to 1976, everyone in our area had to go to Toronto. But the Government has decided to take an established court, which has been in Brampton going on eight years, and establish a brand new court in Mississauga in the riding of Mississauga North. This is a high rent district. It will cost the Government a tremendous amount of money, more than was spent in Brampton. I believe the problem is numbers, because this court services close to 400 applicants every month. It is an extremely busy court. There is room in the building in Brampton to expand and this would cost much less than it is costing in Mississauga. Yet the Government made this decision to move the court. It will cost the Government a tremendous additional amount of money. The location of this court in Brampton is central to the areas it services. This court is now being moved to the south end of the area that it serves.

In the limited time I have I want to talk about the Department of National Revenue for a moment. I guess this Department is known in Canada, quite rightly, as the most effective collection agency in the country. I do not think there is any doubt about that. It is, "You are found guilty and you must prove your innocence later on." These people from Revenue Canada just come in and grab the money.
There is a very disturbing procedure going on in our country today. I am very concerned, as I know a number of my colleagues are. The auditing force of this Department is-and 1 will use the term advisedly-harassing the farming community in Canada. We hear the auditors are in British Columbia now auditing farmers. They have been into Ontario. I can give an example of an individual who was setting up an operation which would eventually have turned into a full-time one. He had received funding from the Federal Business Development Bank. He set up what I and many consider to be a very fine operation. The Department of Revenue did its audit, checking back five years. It forced the individual into bankruptcy. The Department completely destroyed this individual and his operation. The Department forced him to sell his farm at a much lower rate than it was worth, and it forced him to sell good top breeding stock at bankrupt sale prices. This forced him to the wall, and now we have an individual, who was preparing to go into a full-time operation and was deriving some of his revenue elsewhere, who is now completely defeated. He is disspirited. The Department of National Revenue did a real number on this individual, instead of trying to cooperate and help him. That situation is being repeated time and time again.
In Farm and Country, for Tuesday, March 22, 1983, the headline on page 3 reads, "Farmers battle tax grab." This article is about farmers being put upon by the Department of National Revenue. subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have an opportunity today to express a few thoughts regarding the supplementary borrowing authority which the Government is seeking through Bill C-143.
I believe the proper allocation of authority is vital to the survival of Parliament. By whose authority then are expenditures to be approved and laws made? Is it to be done according to the traditions of this country and of other representative democracies throughout the free world? Or is it to be done through Orders in Council in the lofty ivory tower of the Finance Minister? No, Mr. Speaker I think not. It is to be discussed here in the House of Commons before people elected by the citizens of this country where decisions should be made to safeguard the best interests of the populace in mind. These decisions are not-I repeat-not to be made with the narrow, partisan interests of the governing Party in mind. Yet, time and time again in the House, we see gross examples of political engineering and maneuvering instead of face-to-face negotiating on these very important points of borrowing authority and expenditure approval. Would any self-respecting bank manager lend money without having a fair idea of where that money
Borrowing Authority
is going and how it would be paid back? Of course not. Yet the Finance Minister (Mr. Lalonde) hides behind his friendly smile and assures the House that this budget will be coming soon.
We are getting rather tired of being assured. Why not do things in the proper order and let us know how these moneys will be spent before requesting capital for, as the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) puts it, "prudent financial housekeeping". Any of our nation's homemakers would say that they would never stay afloat with this kind of financial housekeeping.
I want to focus on a few more remarks made by the Minister of State for Finance in defence of the Government's request for additional borrowing authority. The Minister's remarks on Thursday of last week seemed to indicate that he is satisfied with the amount of time which has been taken in debate and in committee on Bill C-143. We on this side are not because too many questions remain.
The Minister of State appears deeply concerned that he will not have the necessary capital to handle, as he puts it, "heavy tax refunds". This is rather interesting. Let me remind my hon. colleague that income tax refunds are funds which have already been paid to the Government. Where have they disappeared to? We do not even receive interest on the millions of dollars that are deducted at source during the previous year. This is a financial bonanza for the Government and one of the few sources of income on which its borrowing costs are nil. Yet it cannot even put aside for future reimbursement the small percentage of income tax received which is earmarked for refunds. No, it takes those funds as well and throws them into the trough for any and all Government enterprises to dip into.
It is rather like a lawyer who takes his client's cash to the racetrack. He throws it down on PetroCan in the fifth, Dome in the ninth, and loses his shirt. The only difference is that lawyers can be disbarred. Governments can carry on until their mandate is up, sinking more and more into the comfortable ooze of authority. Hopefully, the client-the citizens of Canada-will call a halt to the game-playing in the very next election. In any case, we in the Opposition are still wondering how the money requested will be spent. It is true that we do have the Estimates. We see the requirements for funding for the Small Business Investment Grant Program and the NEED Program which should ensure a few more Liberal votes. But these programs fail to come to the heart of the problem.
Why are such programs needed? A healthy economy would cure unemployment problems and ensure the development of a prosperous small business sector. However, band-aid programs aside, we are still awaiting the bag of tricks forthcoming from the Minister of Finance. After all, it is in the budget that we see not only the proposed expenditures but how that money will be raised. We shall see what new and devious schemes will be proposed to squeeze yet more funds from the depleted pockets of Canadians from coast to coast.
If we see wonderful and equitable programs emerging from this budget, if creative means are revealed therein which point the way toward economic recovery and a loosening of the

March 28, 1983
Borrowing Authority
regulatory stranglehold on free enterprise, then we shall wholeheartedly approve such expenditures as will be required to meet the needs of these programs. But we will definitely not give voluntary blanket authority to patchwork, stop-gap, finger-in-the-dyke borrowing. We will not do so when one out of every four dollars raised is used to service the national debt.
Any business which operates in this fashion would be long out of business, with padlocks on the doors and plywood on the windows. The Government cannot operate indefinitely on such a huge deficit. Where does it stop? There are too many handouts and too many golden handshakes. Until it stops, the deficit will continue to grow, until eventually our citizens are taxed to death, the nation goes bankrupt and our dollars will become worthless souvenirs, like the deutschemark of bygone days when a wheelbarrelful would buy a loaf of bread.
As was indicated last week, supposedly in defence of Government monetary policy, Cabinet committees are taking responsibility for expenditure management, following guidelines set out by the Lambert Commission. Glowing words were spoken about checks and balances on spending. If these checks and balances are in place and functioning, why did the Auditor General have so much to say in his recent report?
There was more than one indictment of overspending in Government Departments, thus making a mockery of such statements by the Minister of State for Finance as:
The Treasury Board rigorously examines all requests for spending authority by Government departments and agencies. It is constantly on the lookout for inefficiency or impropriety and screens the submissions it receives very carefully.
If such were the case, would the deficit be what it is today?
In the past few weeks, we have heard abundant eloquence from the Government benches justifying the supplemental borrowing authority on the grounds that it is inevitable spending, and that they have somehow done their best and we should accept it. Well, their best is certainly not good enough.
Figures abound to confirm the fact that Government spending has risen much faster than the Consumer Price Index or the Gross National Product. There can be no arguing there. Therefore, why will the Government not give clear and honest answers about why these funds are needed instead of generating vague responses about new programs and seasonal needs? The citizens of Canada are entitled to a fair debate on this issue. Were we elected in order to sit here and watch while their best interests are continually shoved in the background for the purposes of expediency? Is not the whole purpose of Parliament to have such discussion? Without responsible debate we might just as well shut this place down. Without input from elected representatives, our country will eventually be run by a Cabinet committee advising a Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with his emperor-like powers. How close are we to getting to that stage right now?
It was pointed out last week by my hon. colleague, the Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), that the reasoning for deficit spending is a fallacious one and that going deeper and deeper into debt will not help bring about economic prosperity. To that opinion, I add my overwhelming support.
We hear about finance companies which consolidate one's debts by substituting several small payments into one, huge crippling one. Any way one looks at it, one is still in debt. Similarly, adding to the deficit is economic suicide, yet in seeking this supplemental borrowing authority, the Government is doing just that.
Deficits are only short-term and meant to provide funds for programs to stimulate industry and commerce. That is the platform of my friends to the left, and increasingly of my hon. colleagues across the floor who seek to imitate them. However, that is not my Party's policy. We endeavour to cut spending, cut borrowing and cut the deficit because it is a Canadian tradition. That is how our forefathers operated. They built this country up by the free enterprise system and the cash payment system. It worked for them.
Let us not turn this country into another Sweden where free enterprise is virtually dead and where the tax burden is indeed unbearable. That is where we are headed with a Government that borrows increasingly and expects carte blanche to do so.
In conclusion, it is my belief that the Government must exercise more responsibility in dealing with the financial affairs of this nation. One way for it to do so is to determine now that it will make an effort to cut down on the deficit, first, by cleaning house and following the recommendations of the Auditor General. The second way is to encourage participation of Parliament in fiscal affairs and by declining to muzzle dissident voices through premature closure on Bills such as C-143. After all, the welfare of Canadians is at stake.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a privilege to stand today to speak to Bill C-143, and particularly the amendment which has been proposed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). Bill C-143, an interim borrowing Bill, comes in two parts. There is $5 billion for the ongoing expenses to cover the shortfall in federal revenue until the end of this fiscal year. Then we are being asked by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) to do an unprecedented thing, and that is, to provide through this borrowing authority $14 billion which is really, if one looks at the Estimates in the Blue Book, the shortfall in Government revenue for the first seven months of the fiscal year, from the month of April through to the end of October. The Minister comes in blatantly asking for this kind of borrowing authority from the House of Commons, from the people who are representing, or supposed to be representing, their constituents at home, when he is probably two weeks away from a budget that will tell the people what the $14 billion is going to be spent on.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South has clearly stated in the amendment that we will authorize borrowing authority for $1 to the Government, forcing the Government to be accountable to the people so that when they do need the money and they are prepared to tell us what this money is going to be spent on, they will then come back to the



March 28, 1983

House of Commons and to the elected representatives of the people across the country, and say, "This is what we need the money for and this is how we are going to spend it."
Mr. Speaker, it is becoming increasingly frustrating to sit in this House and to have a Government so callous and so brazen that it would come in with this Bill C-143. It does not even shock people anymore that a Minister of Finance would ask this House to willy-nilly pass a borrowing authority Bill that will give him $14 billion for the next fiscal year. This in essence gives him carte blanche to spend the money the way he wants to until the end of October, with no accountability to the taxpayer or to the people of this country. Imagine asking for this sum of money two weeks before he brings down a budget that will tell us how he is going to spend the money!
I had the pleasure of speaking a little while ago to one of my constituents in Fort McMurray who is a true pioneer, Clare Peden, who settled the northern country, who has worked with his hands, who drove a CAT 400 miles through the bush breaking trail so that he could go up and start a construction firm in Fort McMurray years ago, years before there was an oil-sands plant. He has slowly seen his tax dollar, his way of life and his confidence in the Government absolutely and totally destroyed because of actions like this.
I urge all Members, from the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party, to listen to what your constituents are saying to you. They are saying: "Enough is enough!" The waste of spending millions and millions of dollars in advertising across the country saying our energy dollars are working and we are only that far from energy self-sufficiency in this country is beyond belief.
The Government is wasting millions and millions of dollars doing studies to find out why the economy is stagnating. The economy is stagnating in Canada because the present Liberal Government has an attitude similar to that of the present Minister of Finance who says: "Hey, we can borrow $14 billion. We will not even tell the people of Canada. We will not even tell the taxpayer in Canada where that money is going to be spent. They do not need to know. We will tell them when we are good and ready." That is what the present Government is saying, and all Members should recognize that. That is what the Minister is saying when he requests from this House the authority to go out and borrow $14 billion.
1 know, and all Members of this House know, that to operate a Government or to operate a business, there are times when you have to borrow money. Of course you have to borrow on your assets, you have to borrow on your projected revenues, you have to borrow to run the Government. We recognize that. But it is discourteous and it is totally ignorant for a Minister of Finance to come forward and say that the Government wants to borrow $14 billion, and when asked what it is going to use the $14 billion for, to intimate that it is none of our business.
My colleague who spoke just before me asked how one could go to a bank and expect to borrow money and not tell the bank manager what it was needed for. It is the bank's money. The bank manager represents the bank. The bank represents shareholders, it is their money and they want to know what the
Borrowing Authority
borrower is going to use the money for. I recently made a loan at the bank. They wanted detailed copy of how the money was going to be used and how I was going to pay it back, where the revenue was coming from. They wanted to know the cashflow.
The people of Canada want to know where the $14 billion is going to go. They do not want the Members who are sitting in this House to give the Minister of Finance carte blanche authority to spend $14 billion on the kinds of things that he has spent it on in the past. They want to know if he has an oil company in mind that the Government wants to buy. They want to know if he wants to buy a pulp and paper mill. They want to know if the money is going to be used to bail out a Massey-Ferguson or a Ford or a GM. They want to know if the money is going to be used to assist the farmer, to assist the unemployed, and they have a right to know because you and I as Members of Parliament representing constituents are accountable to those constituents. We have to go home and say to our constituents, yes or no, this is why it is being spent and this is why it was authorized.
We in this House know that this Bill is going to pass. We know that it is going to go through because there is a majority Government. I have yet to see a Member from the Government benches stand up, give us an analysis and tell us where this $14 billion that is being requested is going to go. All we are asking in this amendment is that the Hon. Members on all sides of the House vote yes to the first part, the $5 billion, which has to be allocated to finish off this fiscal year, but that the $14 billion be denied that Minister of Finance with an insatiable appetite for spending money. We ask that it be denied now, and when it is required, that a Bill be brought before this House detailing exactly where this money is going to be spent so that we can then go back to our constituents and be able to account for it.
It is paramount that this amendment go through, and it should go through with all Hon. Members' blessings because, in the final analysis, our duty is to our country, our duty is to our constituency, and then our duty is to our Party, and it is not the other way around.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to read briefly from a letter received from a valued constituent, Mr. Reed Naylor of Okanagan Falls. He says in part:
There are obvious areas of out-and-out waste and it is rapidly ruining us. 1 still hope that someone will organize a blacklist of Government waste to which anyone who sees examples may contribute. If such a program could be made to snowball, it might develop sufficient credence to indicate to Government some of the flagrant absurdities of their wasteful policies. It beats me to see my taxes spent on repeated advertising on CTV by federal Departments such as Environment, Metric Commission, Parks Canada, etc. etc. I counted five in one 60-minute period a few days ago.
It is no wonder the subject of waste in constantly raised. No wonder the subject of Government advertising often occupies the attention of Members. Spending by the Metric Commission on a program that practically no one in Canada wants is repeatedly raised. We are becoming a nation of cynics. The

March 28, 1983
Borrowing Authority
Government is asking for an unreasonable blank cheque so that it can continue its extravagance. It is creating an image, and people no longer believe in the integrity of Government.
Last Friday afternoon I flew from Vancouver to Penticton. A young lady sat beside me. She was from New Brunswick, now living in Coquitlam where she is working for the provincial Government as a dietician. This lady supports her parents who still live in New Brunswick. She made a remark that I believe is the typical reaction of the majority of Canadians. She said she was willing to make sacrifices for her country and was prepared to accept a salary freeze if necessary, but that she was offended by what was going on in Ottawa where restraint is spoken about but the Government is not prepared to restrain its own spending.
That is a common reaction in Canada today. People are prepared to sacrifice for their country, but they are offended by a Government that carries on a practice of waste, extravagance and patronage. It looks after its interests and those of its friends, to the disadvantage of those not so classified. This is why we are becoming a nation of cynics.
Just last week in Penticton, which is in my riding, Greenwood Forest Products was put into receivership. This was a busy milling operation, the largest employer in the area. It had a record of innovation. It was a productive enterprise, one that had developed a lucrative European market for lodge-pole pine panelling, competing with Scandinavian products.
That company had too much debt at too high an interest rate. The shutdown threw 250 employees out of work, placing them on the unemployment roll. This will have a domino effect on logging contractors, suppliers, engineering firms, in fact, the whole community. This is the most catastrophic incident to happen in the area.
Why did it happen? One reason over and above what I have mentioned was that the assistance offered to Greenwood Forest Products by the federal Government through its Enterprise Development Program was too slow in coming and imposed conditions just not acceptable to the parties.
This is in comparison to what the Government of Canada did for Maislin Trucking of Montreal. It guaranteed a $34 million loan with almost no strings attached. The treatment of Greenwood Forest Products has been unworthy and discriminatory. No wonder people are becoming cynical with this uneven treatment by Government, a Government that looks after its friends to the exclusion of those not in that category. Maislin had friends in Government. Greenwood Forest Products did not have friends of equal influence. It is this type of situation which offends Canadians and makes them cynical about Government.
The Canadian Federation of Independent Businesses disclosed that close to half of Canada's unemployed are former employees of small and medium-size businesses. It conducted a survey which showed that 51 per cent of responding businesses had reduced the number of their employees since early 1981. It is significant that most businesses that responded had reduced salary demands, below 6 per cent; 38 per cent gave no salary increase to their employees; and 6 per cent had actually reduced wages. Compare that to the federal Government's six
and five approach for which it takes credit for all kinds of miraculous happenings in the economy. It has killed the economy. It makes it impossible for economic activity to take place. The Government says the six and five programs has broken the back of inflation. The other day I said it was like a farmer going into his chicken house, killing all his chickens and then taking credit for the fact that the weasels are no longer getting his eggs.
Mr. Bulloch says the private sector is leading the Government in restraint and wages. He points the finger at the Government in other ways. He said and I quote from the newspaper account:
Mr. Bulloch did say that while the recession was worldwide, "much of the cause has also been the result of a combination of damaging federal policies and intergovernmental bickering." He condemned the "collection of ill-conceived and ill-timed tax proposals" ... and the malignant growth of the federal budget deficit.
It has an impact on people in many different ways. A widow telephoned me the other day to say that she is receiving phonecalls from a collection agency about her son's student loan. Her son made payments as long as he was working, but he is now out of work. He advised the bank that he could not make further payments until he resumed work. The bank sent the official letter, after which it can call on the Government to pay the loan under the Government guarantee. The Government then proceeds to put the matter in the hands of a collection agency. This collection agency is saying to this recently widowed friend of mine who is living on a widow's allowance, "You have a responsibility. Mortgage your house so you can pay off your son's loan. It is your responsibility to look after this." I suppose none of us likes the fact that there are 100,000 student loans in default. That represents something like $200 million. However, I do not believe that the Government should be so cruel and so insensitive to the realities of life that it will put a collection agency onto a widow who is a responsible person, and suggest that she has an obligation to pay her son's indebtedness.
I think that is symptomatic of something which is happening in the country, that we have a Government which is out of control and which is putting the squeeze on everyone but itself. In so doing it is making, as I said before, cynics of Canadians.
