Mr. Speaker, the blanket which the federal Government is placing over Canadians is going to smother a society which we have known for 100 years. It is a great misfortune that Members on the Government side are not prepared to rise and take a stand on issues which are going to destroy our country if something is not done about it. When this Prime Minister took office, Mr. Speaker, 15 per cent of the GNP was all that was required to finance Government's operations. This year the expenditure will take 23 per cent of the GNP. The increased costs of financing Government since 1968 have multiplied 12 times. Canadians, I believe, are now starting to realize just exactly what is happening. For a
March 28, 1983

long time a lot of Canadians would tell politicians they would far rather have a Government going broke than their businesses being broke. Now, Mr. Speaker, we are finding out they are both broke. The total debt for which the federal Government is responsible is approximately $250 billion. People are now starting to realize what the consequences of that may be.
A few months ago the Government deficit was supposed to be $10.6 billion. Then the Minister of Finance said it would be $18 billion. Then it got to be $23 billion. Now at the end of this fiscal year we are finding it is well over $27 billion. Never in the history of Canada have Estimates been so far out of kilter. We must hold the Government responsible for this and we must hold the Minister of Finance responsible. This kind of attitude toward inappropriate action on the part of any governing body will ensure that we are going to enter into a disastrous situation.
Who is going to pull Canada out of the problems with which we have to deal? Government expenditures have outgrown and outstripped the growth in GNP. Let me impress upon you, Mr. Speaker, that deficit spending is just deferred taxation. What we are really doing is shoving a debt load onto our children and our grandchildren. They are going to have a great deal of difficulty trying to deal with it, and I am sure that they are going to be very unforgiving when they find out exactly what is being done to them. We have this rapid escalation of debt, yet the Government wants to borrow $14 billion more. My goodness gracious, Mr. Speaker, $1.5 billion in 1968 paid the cost of financing our national debt. Today it is $18.6 billion. That amount does not include any of the costs of our Crown corporations. In 1968, our debt cost 13 cents of every dollar which the Government spent. Today it is 20 cents. This is money which the Government is spending, not just taxation dollars which are taken in.
We must realize, Mr. Speaker, that we are in a terrible situation as far as our balance of finances are concerned and we must be cognizant of that. The Canadian people are now starting to realize just exactly what the situation is. The total debt, as I said earlier, for which the federal Government is responsible, is in the area of $250 billion. If we work that out among our Canadian people, it is $10,000 for every man, woman and child. A family of four, which is the average family in Canada, is facing $40,000 debt because of the position that their federal Government put them into.
The problem, Mr. Speaker, with the taxation policies of the Government, is that it is trying to grab more and more. Just the other day I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) if he would not consider cutting the excise tax on fuel and energy which is required in the production of our food. The Minister retorted, "Well, the Government has to get some money from some place." Far better, Mr. Speaker, for the Government to cut the cloth to fit the pattern. The Government should cut some of the expenditures which are not required. My colleague, from British Columbia mentioned one of them, the Metric Commission, still doling millions and millions of dollars out. There are many other programs over which the Government seems to have no control, or does not seem to have the
Borrowing Authority
desire to exercise control. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), mentioned earlier today the former Auditor General, Mr. Macdonell, who did a tremendous job when he was Auditor General, and he told the Government at that time that to all intents and purposes expenditures were out of control. Nothing has changed since that time. Government expenditure is still out of control. The only difference is that it is worsening, and Government has less control today than it has ever had in Canadian history.
I believe we are falling further and further behind in competition with other nations because of the fact that we are allowing our nation to drift further and further into debt. This national debt is being placed on our businesses, and our businesses are being forced out of business. I fear that if we stay on our present course we will continue to be hewers of wood and drawers of water. It is the responsibility of any Government to establish a climate in which our business community can progress and develop and in turn develop business. Small businesses supply 60 per cent of our jobs in Canada today. If we allow the Government to put the small businesses into bankruptcy, then we are all going to suffer the consequences. What happens when you put small business out of operation? They lay off people. Those people, instead of paying income tax, are then drawing Unemployment Insurance. What a lot of the Government's programs are actually doing is taking people who have been on welfare for a while or have exhausted their UIC benefits, and giving them a job for long enough to qualify for UIC. This is not very productive, Mr. Speaker, and it can be done in a better way. The Government should realize that this is its responsibility, and this is why this Government is being so irresponsible in not recognizing the benefits which can accrue when all Canadians are working together.
I do not think the Government should be asking the Canadian people for another $14 billion because it cannot afford the finance its present debt.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak to this Bill for a few minutes. This borrowing Bill is the fourth of its kind in the past eight months. Since $14 billion of the amount requested is to keep us going for the rest of the year, this Bill amounts to the Government's asking for a blank cheque to keep it going. The Government is asking us for money for programs which it has not even placed before the House, programs which have probably not even been thought of yet. In addition, a large percentage of this money goes to service existing Government debt, a good portion of which was brought about because the Government proceeded for the last 12 or 13 years with very little planning. It has approached government on a kind of day-to-day, session-by-session basis without any long-term planning. So what this Bill is actually doing, Mr. Speaker, is asking the people of Canada to pay for the lack of planning by this Government.

March 28, 1983
Borrowing Authority
There are other examples of bad planning by Government which I could give this House, Mr. Speaker. One year after the present Government of Saskatchewan came into power, it had established a deficit of $220 million, considerably more in one year than all the previous Governments of Saskatchewan had managed to accumulate in the previous 77 years. But without planning, Government expenditures get out of hand. This Government's spending record is like a snowball going downhill. We have all seen those comic strips where a snowmobile starts small at the tope of the hill and as it goes down it picks up increasing amounts of snow, until at the bottom of the hill it ends up looking like a very large snowball. This snowball analogy is very apt, Mr. Speaker, because the big spending started back in 1970. That is when it started to snowball down the hill. The present administration had regular expenditures with very little planning until we got to the point, the bottom of the hill, that it had a huge deficit.
Just as a matter of interest, Mr. Speaker, back in 1973 the accumulated deficit of this Government was $51 billion; in 1976, $59 billion; in 1979, $98 billion; in 1982, $134 billion. But that does not include all those other debts the Government has run up, the debts of Crown corporations for which the Government is responsible, the letters of credit for which the Government is responsible, or letters of comfort as they are sometimes called. If you added all those together, the deficit would be well over $200 billion, Mr. Speaker. In 1970 we had an accumulated deficit of $900 per capita. By 1982 it reached $3,883 per capita. In other words, this particular Government has increased the per capita debt four times.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there are times when deficits have a value. But what was the value of a deficit in the period from 1970-71 to 1974? There was no reason for deficits at that time. Right now deficit spending has a possibility of increasing the number of jobs. But basically we should use deficits only when they are of direct value to the economy, and that is the only time.
I know our Party is often called the spending Party. Well, as an example of what good spenders we are, I would point again to Saskatchewan and the 30 years of CCF and NDP Government. In that period of time it established an outstanding record of social services and expenditures that were good for the Province and for the country. It made those expenditures without once establishing a deficit. That is a good use of money, Mr. Speaker.
In the same period of time the federal Government increased the per capita deficit of the people of Canada fourfold from under $1,000 to approximately $4,000.
I should like to return to the reasons for the borrowing request, Mr. Speaker. It is required for programs that have not been placed before the House. An increased amount of money is to be expended on the railways, and I agree that there is a need for that but not at the expense of the farmers. The Government plans to ask farmers to pay for part of that rail expansion. It has already committed a lot of money to the
railway, but has not come before Parliament with this proposition. That is one reason it is asking for more money, and there are other reasons such as Mirabel and Pickering and other bad expenditures made in the past. If the Government planned its spending better, then there would be no need for these borrowing Bills.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate on Bill C-143, the supplemental borrowing authority Bill to authorize the Government to borrow up to an additional $5 billion in new money for the current 1982-83 fiscal year. It will also provide further authority to the Government to borrow up to $14 billion for fiscal year 1983-84, for a total, Mr. Speaker of some $19 billion.
Without question, Mr. Speaker, the total borrowing authority of $19 billion granted in this Bill is the largest borrowing in our country's 116 year history. To add fuel to the fire, Mr. Speaker, this is the second time this year that the Government has sought to increase authority by more than the requirements that had been projected in its most recent financial forecast. The deficit today Mr. Speaker, is 28 per cent of all expenditures. In other words, for every $4 the Government spends, it must borrow a little more than $ 1.
Mr. Speaker, the Government keeps telling us that the federal debt is $134 billion. However, as the Hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) and I have stated on earlier occasions, and when one adds in the total debt of the Crown corporations of $55 billion and the $49 billion in pension funds that the Government has appropriated, the total debt is closer to $240 billion.
The June and October budgets of 1982 failed to provide economic and fiscal projections for the current fiscal year. Experts tell us that that is dangerous because it creates uncertainty and leads to unwarranted speculation and disruptive speculation in the financial markets as to the state of the federal Government's finances.
No banker, Mr. Speaker, would grant a line of credit to a financially crippled business that refused to provide cash flow projections. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, a private industry or enterprise with revenue that equalled only 70 per cent of expenditures and a gross debt that was more than triple the value of its assets, would be forced into bankruptcy. The federal Government, Mr. Speaker, cannot declare bankruptcy because it has no place to file.
There is no question that the poor economic performance will continue to have a negative impact on the finances of the Government, as the cost of social assistance rises and revenues stagnate or fall. Any recovery that may occur, Mr. Speaker, is likely to be a weak recovery, and as such will only have a moderate impact on the current fiscal dilemma. Even if we have a moderate recovery it may not be enough to bring the federal books into balance.
Unless measures are taken to control spending and to create economic growth, it can be expected that the present situation will not readily improve. By controlling spending, Mr. Speaker, I realize that the Government is committed to carrying out
March 28, 1983

its obligations in financing our important social programs, such as Old Age Security, Spouse's Allowance, medicare, and many other worthwhile programs. These are obligations and duties that must not be reneged upon. But, Mr. Speaker, there are many, many other areas of spending that should be seriously looked at, that should either be curtailed or should be eliminated entirely.
One only has to go through the Auditor General's annual Report to see areas of unproductive spending, areas of mismanagement, areas of unaccountability and cost over-runs which, when totalled, amount to millions and billions of taxpayers' dollars wasted and gone down the drain.
I am not here to castigate and chastise individuals or Department officials, Mr. Speaker. I believe that most of them are dedicated people and are trying their best to do the best job possible. However, Mr. Speaker, because the money that they handle and the money that is their responsibility to spend wisely is not really their own, I do not believe there is the same judicial care exercised to spend the taxpayers' money more prudently.
I have in my possession a document that really spells out this problem in detail, but in the brief time at my disposal in this debate, it will not be possible for me to read this document into the record because of its length. However, perhaps I could draw the attention of the Chair and the Members to a couple of examples. One has to do with over-runs-spending over budget.
Environment Canada, experienced cost over-runs on 153 out of the total 223 projects to the amount of $283 million. This is a glaring example of poor budget planning, which would have resulted in wholesale firings if it had happened in private industry. But we all know that public servants rarely get fired. If something goes wrong, the punishment is usually a promotion to get him or her out of the Department.
In the other extreme, Mr. Speaker, on July 1, 1982, two days after announcing the need for more restraint, the Government paid $430,000 to provide 16 cities with fireworks. Really, Mr. Speaker, where is the common sense?
Common sense should tell us that we are heading for rocky shoals if this trend in spending continues. It is a case, Mr. Speaker of this Government's continuing to flounder around, pulling the wrong levers and greasing the wrong skids. The Government must readjust its priorities to get our economy rolling again. Money must be spent wisely to get our economy back on track. We must regain our strong economic base. Our industry must modernize in order to grow and expand. The Government should be encouraging such undertakings, not penalizing businesses with disincentives and by drowning incentive by the myriads of discouraging regulations that private enterprise is forced to contend with.
There must be a dovetailing and equity and partnership between business and Government. Harmony will bring about better economic results while, on the other hand, working at loggerheads with each other only ends in chaos and bankruptcy.
Over the years we have heard common arguments used by the Liberals to defend the Government's record on spending,
Borrowing Authority
debt and the deficit. One of these is, "Deficit spending is good for economic growth". Common sense should tell them that deficits do not necessarily occur as a consequence of measures to promote economic growth. The truth is that most of the existing deficit is the result of the failure to achieve economic growth. For example, in November of 1981 economic growth was projected by the then Minister of Finance to be 2.2 per cent. The projected deficit was $10.5 billion. In June of 1982 the Government predicted a negative growth of 2 per cent, and the projected deficit was forecast to be $19.6 billion. For the fiscal year 1982-83 the Government is forecasting a decline of
4.4	per cent, and the expected deficit will likely be around $30 billion.
It can be readily seen, Mr. Speaker, as the deficit has grown from year to year, that Canadians have become more and more aware of the damage that continuous deficits inflict upon the economy. We must be aware as well, Mr. Speaker, that our excessive borrowing is one of the reasons for the weak dollar and for the recent very high interest rates that have been necessary to support the dollar.
Another fallacy, Mr. Speaker, that we hear from the Government is, and I quote, "There is a deficit because of the positive initiatives the Liberals have taken over the years to assist Canadians." The truth is, Mr. Speaker, that the many examples of unnecessary spending by the Liberals have been an unnecessary drain on the Treasury. That red herring, Mirabel Airport, has cost the taxpayers of Canada $700 million. As I mentioned earlier in my speech, the Government has consistently failed to exercise adequate cost control on projects and programs. It was discovered in October, 1979 that cost over-runs for ongoing projects initiated by the Liberals totalled $1.1 billion.
In 1978, the Unemployment Insurance Commission paid $290 million to those not legally entitled to receive benefits. Another fallacy projected by this Government is: "There is nothing wrong with having a large national debt. We only owe the money to ourselves, and there are assets to offset the debt."
The major problem with the Government's debt is that it must be serviced. One tax dollar in four is used to pay interest on the debt. Interest on the public debt will cost the taxpayers of Canada $16.7 billion in the fiscal year 1982-1983. That represents $700 per capita or $1,800 per taxpayer. The assets of the Government are dwarfed by its debt. In March, 1982, the Government had $40 billion in assets, compared to a total official gross national debt of $134 billion, which we know is not quite right, it is closer to $200 billion to $250 billion.
Another fallacy enunciated by the Government is: "There's nothing wrong with a short-term deficit." The federal Government has not balanced its books since 1970, and it will not do so in the next five years. The Liberals have maintained since 1970 that the deficit is only a short-term problem. There is nothing short-term about 17 years.
